The update adds lyric merchandise that artists can sell to fans via the Musixmatch app and website, a Wallet tracking earnings, merchandise sales and referrals in a single view, and an Insights & Analytics dashboard combining streaming activity, follower data and lyric views across a catalog. Co-president Marco Paglia said lyrics are one of the most powerful ways people connect with music, and the new tools let artists see how and where fans engage with their lyrics and earn from that engagement directly. The platform's AI Enrichment tool transcribes lyrics and synchronises them line by line and word by word, and produces AI-generated meanings and themes for songs. Artists also get access to Music Lens, an AI agent unveiled in November 2025 that helps them explore their catalogs and uncover insights. The planned AI licensing option follows deals Musixmatch signed in October 2025 with the publishing arms of all three majors, Sony Music Publishing, Universal Music Publishing Group and Warner Chappell Music, giving it access to catalogs of more than 15 million works to develop non-generative AI services. Musixmatch did not name the AI platforms that would license lyrics through the Wallet or give a launch date. In October Musixmatch acquired Music Reports, the company behind the Songdex copyright registry, describing the deal as making it a full-stack rights and royalties platform.

articles.title: Believe fully acquires Lili Louise Musique, parent of French indie tot Ou tard
articles.description: Believe has fully acquired Lili Louise Musique, parent of French indie label tot Ou tard, becoming sole shareholder, announced November 25. Founder Vincent Frerebeau stays at the helm and keeps full control of artistic direction; terms were not disclosed. The deal completes a partnership begun in 2018, when Believe bought a 49% stake from Wagram Music for EUR 12.3 million.
articles.body: The Paris-headquartered company announced the deal on Wednesday, November 25, calling it 'a natural continuation' of a partnership that began in 2018, when Believe acquired a 49% stake in Lili Louise Musique from Wagram Music. Believe did not disclose the financial terms of the transaction, and founder Vincent Frerebeau will continue to lead the group with full control over its directions and artistic choices. The deal covers all of Lili Louise Musique's activities, including tot Ou tard, live performance company Zouave, publishing arm LLM, the innovative-projects company Guess What, and stakes in live music company Uni-t. Each brand will keep its identity, organisation, teams, premises and corporate culture, along with artistic, editorial and strategic autonomy, Believe said. Frerebeau said that in a market moving faster and faster, the ability to think long-term becomes even more valuable, and the new chapter protects what makes the group unique. Tot Ou tard, described by MBW in 2018 as the second-biggest independent label in France behind Because Music, celebrated its 30th anniversary this year, with best-known signings including Vianney, Vincent Delerm and Shaka Ponk. Believe's pre-IPO filings showed the company paid EUR 12.3 million for its original 49% stake. The deal follows Believe's October move to expand Romain Vivien's role, putting the Global Head of Music in direct charge of its EMEA, Americas and APAC regions. Believe itself was taken private by the Upbeat BidCo consortium of founder Denis Ladegaillerie, the EQT X fund and TCV funds, which acquired around 95% of its share capital in 2024 and completed a squeeze-out, with the company delisted from Euronext Paris in August 2025. Believe operates in more than 50 countries and employs more than 2,000 people.

articles.title: Beatles attraction at 3 Savile Row, site of the band's final public concert, approved by London council
articles.description: Westminster City Council approved plans on November 24 for a Beatles visitor attraction at 3 Savile Row, the former Apple Corps HQ where the band played its final public concert on the rooftop in January 1969. The attraction, 'The Beatles at 3 Savile Row', is expected to open in 2027, with archive exhibitions, a recreated basement studio and rooftop access. Apple Corps CEO Tom Greene said visitors will feel they are sitting behind the band as they played their final show.
articles.body: Westminster City Council's Planning Committee signed off on the plans on Tuesday, November 24, for the project Apple Corps first unveiled in May under the name 'The Beatles at 3 Savile Row'. The attraction is expected to open in 2027, with exhibitions drawn from the Apple Corps archives, a recreated version of the basement recording studio, and access to the rooftop. The Beatles worked on 'Let It Be' in the building's basement studio in 1969, and on January 30 that year John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr, joined by Billy Preston, played on the building's roof in the band's last public live performance. The rooftop set was later featured in Peter Jackson's 2021 documentary 'Get Back', which won five Emmy Awards. Apple Corps CEO Tom Greene said visitors will feel they are sitting behind the Beatles as they played their fabled final show, before stepping onto probably the most famous terrace in the world. The front of the building will be returned to how it looked and felt in 1969, right down to the Apple green carpet, supplemented with the latest AV technology, and the company wants to host bookable evening events plus a cafe and bar in the basement for ticket holders. Draft conditions in Westminster's planning papers, reported by the BBC ahead of the vote, included a ban on live music on the rooftop terrace. The BBC also reported Apple Corps expects as many as 900 visitors a day on weekdays and 1,140 on weekends, while the Savile Row Bespoke Association objected, warning the street's narrow sidewalks could become congested. Greene told the committee the building was sold in the mid-1970s after the breakup and Apple Corps was excited to buy back the headlease, noting fans still congregate outside every day, and pointed to a letter Paul McCartney sent the committee. In October Apple Corps announced plans to take over The Beatles Story in Liverpool and move it to a 100,000-square-foot city centre site in 2028, and in August Universal Music Group signed a global partnership with Apple Corps covering Beatles merchandise, licensing and e-commerce. Sam Mendes' four Beatles films are set for release in April 2028.

articles.title: Mary Bono asks appeals court to overturn Cher's win in Sonny Bono song royalties fight
articles.description: Mary Bono, widow of Sonny Bono, has asked the US Ninth Circuit to overturn Cher's 2025 court win over royalties from Sonny's songs, filing her opening brief on November 24. A federal judge ruled in November 2025 that Cher remains entitled to half of Sonny's income from songs written before February 1, 1974, including 'I Got You Babe', and awarded her over $187,000 plus interest. Mary Bono argues Sonny could not sign away rights that did not exist in his lifetime and that Cher has 'already received nearly fifty years of royalties'.
articles.body: Mary Bono's lawyers at Donahue Fitzgerald filed her 59-page opening brief with the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on Tuesday, November 24. It asks the court to rule that the US rights and royalties in Sonny's songs now belong to his widow and four children 'free and clear' of the rights granted to Cher under the pair's 1978 divorce settlement. A federal judge ruled in November 2025 that Cher remains entitled to half of Sonny's income from songs he wrote before February 1, 1974, including 'I Got You Babe', and in a final judgment on November 26, 2025 awarded her more than $187,000 plus interest for withheld publishing royalties. The dispute turns on copyright termination: in 2016 Mary Bono, Cesare and Chianna served notice reclaiming, on behalf of all five heirs, the rights Sonny had granted to his music publishers in 1966, with effective dates from 2018 to 2026. The heirs then stopped paying Cher her 50% share, arguing the reclaimed rights belonged entirely to them, and Cher sued in October 2021. The brief's main argument is that Sonny could not sign away rights that did not yet exist: 'Sonny could not have entered into an agreement in 1978 to transfer a property right that came into existence, and vested in the Heirs, not him, in 2016.' By MBW's calculation, the judge's ruling leaves Cher with around 45 cents of each dollar of income, up from 31.5 cents before the terminations, because she now gets half of the heirs' income including the reclaimed publishers' 30-cent share. As a fallback, the brief argues only the publishers' share should go to the heirs alone, leaving Cher with the same 31.5 cents she received before, which it says is what Cher herself testified she wants: 'I should get what I've always gotten.' Sonny died in 1998 without a will, and his heirs are Mary Bono and his four children Christine, Chaz, Cesare and Chianna. Cher sold her rights under the divorce settlement in January 2023, effective July 1, 2022, to Irving Azoff's Iconic Artists Group, though the judge ruled royalties remain payable to Cher. Cher is also appealing the July 2026 denial of her request for attorneys' fees, and the Ninth Circuit has consolidated the two appeals.

articles.title: Downtown Music Publishing hires ex-Luminate exec Helena Kosinski and Armada's Michel Peek for international expansion
articles.description: Downtown Music Publishing has appointed Helena Kosinski as SVP of International Strategy and Business Development and Michel Peek as General Manager of UK & Europe, both newly created roles announced November 25 as part of a new international expansion strategy. Kosinski, formerly of Luminate/MRC Data/Nielsen Music, will lead DMP's international growth from London; Peek, formerly of Armada Music, will run the UK and European push from Virgin Music Group's Amsterdam offices. Peek reports to Kosinski, who reports to DMP president Emily Stephenson.
articles.body: Downtown Music Publishing announced the two newly created roles on Wednesday, November 25, as part of a new international expansion strategy. London-based Kosinski will lead the growth and transformation of the international business, spotting growth opportunities globally, setting DMP's strategy for signing clients and songwriters, and developing partnerships and commercial opportunities. She will report directly to DMP president Emily Stephenson, while Peek will report directly to Kosinski. Kosinski joins from her own consulting company, where she advised data and technology companies on the music business, and previously held executive positions at Luminate and its predecessors MRC Data and Nielsen Music, where she led the international business. Luminate, which powers the Billboard charts, took its current name in 2022, and Kosinski is also chair of the advisory board at Music Technology UK. Peek, based in Virgin Music Group's Amsterdam offices, is tasked with growing DMP's presence in the UK and Europe, building relationships with independent publishers, labels, managers and collecting societies. He joins from Armada Music, where he set up the company's publishing arm in 2018 and served as general manager of Armada Music Publishing; the Amsterdam label, co-founded by Armin van Buuren, formed its publishing arm in 2024 as part of its acquisition of Cloud 9 Music. The appointments come nine months after Universal Music Group's Virgin Music Group completed its $775 million acquisition of Downtown Music Holdings on February 20, bringing DMP, Songtrust, FUGA, CD Baby and Downtown Artist & Label Services under VMG ownership. DMP's existing international operations include Downtown Music Publishing Africa, launched in May 2025 following the rebrand of Sheer Publishing, which Downtown acquired in 2020. DMP says its clients and songwriters earned 44 nominations at the 2026 Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year for Bad Bunny, whose 'Debi Tirar Mas Fotos' won on February 1, and won 11 awards at the 2025 Latin Grammys. Its catalogues include John Lennon, Atticus Ross and Phish, and in May DMP struck a deal to represent the catalogue of Biz Markie as well as his name, image and likeness rights.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65 after prostate cancer battle
articles.description: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of Duran Duran, has died at 65 after a long battle with metastatic prostate cancer. He died peacefully at home on Monday, November 23, surrounded by his family, his family and former bandmates confirmed in a joint statement released Wednesday, November 25. Taylor co-wrote the band's defining hits including 'Hungry Like the Wolf', 'Rio' and 'Girls on Film', and was inducted with the band into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
articles.body: Taylor died peacefully at home on Monday, November 23, surrounded by his family, after a 'long and courageous battle' with prostate cancer, his family and former bandmates confirmed in a joint statement released Wednesday, November 25. He was born February 16, 1961, in Tynemouth, England, and as Duran Duran's original guitarist he injected a rock edge into the band's new-wave sound, co-writing defining hits including 'Hungry Like the Wolf', 'Rio', 'Girls on Film' and 'The Reflex'. The band's huge pop hits were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, and Taylor won two Grammys with the group. His cancer diagnosis was revealed publicly on the night of the band's Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction in November 2022, when it emerged he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for four years and could not attend the ceremony. He later released 'Man's a Wolf to Man' in 2023, his first solo album in more than 30 years, and as a solo artist his song 'Take It Easy' reached No. 24 in 1986. Tributes poured in from his bandmates, Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle, among others, and his family asked that in lieu of flowers, fans make donations in his name to Prostate Cancer UK. The news comes two weeks after the band announced that drummer Roger Taylor would step down and retire from music altogether due to worsening tinnitus symptoms. Rolling Stone had covered Taylor extensively, including a 2023 interview in which he reflected on his departure from the band.

articles.title: King Crimson co-founder and drummer Michael Giles dies at 84
articles.description: Michael Giles, the founding drummer and co-founder of King Crimson, has died at 84. He died on Monday, November 23, his label Discipline Global Mobile, founded by bandmate Robert Fripp, announced. Giles played on the band's landmark 1969 debut 'In the Court of the Crimson King' and helped define progressive rock drumming.
articles.body: Giles died on Monday, November 23, and the news was announced by Discipline Global Mobile, the record label founded by his old bandmate Robert Fripp. The label's statement read: 'It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Michael Giles, visionary drummer, composer and co-founder of King Crimson, who died on Monday 23rd November 2026, aged 84.' No cause of death was disclosed. Alongside Fripp, Greg Lake, Ian McDonald and Peter Sinfield, Giles was instrumental in establishing King Crimson as one of the most innovative and influential bands in the history of progressive music. His drumming on the band's landmark 1969 debut 'In the Court of the Crimson King', above all on '21st Century Schizoid Man', set a new standard for rhythmic imagination in rock, and in a 2019 interview with Rolling Stone he reflected on that song's legacy. Giles left the band after its second album and later made the duo album 'McDonald and Giles', did session work and played in the 21st Century Schizoid Band. His influence was cited by later drummers including Neil Peart and Danny Carey, and fans mourning online repeatedly pointed to his jazz-inflected precision and melodic fills. Fripp's tribute was brief: 'Fly well, Michael.' With Giles' death, Fripp is the last surviving original member of King Crimson. His passing was the second major rock death announced on November 25, alongside Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor, who also died aged 65.

articles.title: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie settle bitter Chateau Miraval winery war a decade after split
articles.description: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled their years-long legal battle over Chateau Miraval, the French winery they once co-owned, a decade after their 2016 split. In a joint statement Wednesday, November 25, the actors said: 'We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further.' Terms were not disclosed, and it remains unclear how the settlement affects related litigation involving Pitt and the Stoli Group.
articles.body: Representatives for Pitt, 62, and Jolie, 51, shared a joint statement with media on Wednesday, November 25: 'We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further.' The statement also said that comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are not coming from either of them or anyone close to them. The settlement terms were not disclosed, and it remains unclear how the deal affects ongoing litigation involving Pitt and the Stoli Group. Pitt sued Jolie in 2022, saying she had abandoned an agreement that he would buy her half of Chateau Miraval, a French winery they bought in 2008, by selling her stake to a 'stranger' with a bad reputation. Jolie responded with a $250 million countersuit, claiming Pitt was 'waging a vindictive war against' her and denying she needed his approval to sell. A filing from Jolie in the case surfaced abuse allegations against Pitt, which gave the business dispute a far wider public dimension. Wednesday's settlement brings both Jolie's and Pitt's lawsuits to a close, a decade after the couple split in 2016. The former couple settled their bitter divorce after eight years in December 2024, but the winery fight had continued separately until now. The resolution ends one of Hollywood's longest-running post-split legal battles.

articles.title: Coachella sues Walmart over unauthorised festival merch, citing 'willful and repeated acts'
articles.description: Coachella and promoter Goldenvoice have sued Walmart for trademark infringement, alleging the retailer repeatedly sold unlicensed festival merchandise despite demands to stop dating back to 2017. The complaint, filed Tuesday, November 24 in US District Court for the Central District of California, seeks a temporary restraining order, injunctions and unspecified damages. It cites 12 US trademark registrations covering the Coachella name, 'Chella', the palm tree logo and the festival's Ferris wheel imagery.
articles.body: Coachella Music Festival, LLC and Goldenvoice, LLC, which produces the festival, filed the complaint on Tuesday, November 24, in the US District Court for the Central District of California, naming Walmart Inc. and Wal-Mart.com USA, LLC as defendants. It brings claims of trademark infringement and false designation of origin under the federal Lanham Act, plus unfair competition and misleading advertising claims under California law. The complaint says Walmart, which it describes as 'the world's largest retailer' with more than 4,600 US locations, has repeatedly sold merchandise bearing Coachella's trademarks without a licence, despite demands dating back to 2017 that it stop. The alleged incidents include online listings in June 2017, when Walmart advertised at least 28 clothing items under the Coachella name, apparel sold at the North Indio store in April 2019, and a resumption of sales at the La Quinta store in April 2026. The complaint also cites Instagram videos posted around this year's festival by the Desert Sun, a Palm Springs news outlet, showing tumblers, bottles, wine glasses, tank tops and other merchandise bearing the Coachella marks at Walmart's North Indio store, with the caption 'Who needs the merch tent when you have the North Indio Walmart?' The lawsuit asserts rights in 12 US trademark registrations, covering the Coachella name, Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, 'Chella', the palm tree logo and the festival's Ferris wheel imagery. The plaintiffs, represented by Tucker Ellis LLP, are seeking a temporary restraining order as well as preliminary and permanent injunctions, unspecified damages, and a jury trial. The complaint also cites trademark claims brought against Walmart by Nike, Yeti Coolers, Crocs, Vans and Deckers, which owns Hoka, Teva and Ugg. Coachella has announced its 2027 lineup, including Dua Lipa, Madonna, Steve Lacy, Tame Impala, SZA, Don Toliver and Daddy Yankee.

articles.title: Ariana Grande announces 'Eternal Sunshine' tour documentary and concert film for Peacock
articles.description: Ariana Grande has confirmed a two-part film project for Peacock: the documentary 'The Eternal Sunshine Diaries: The Making of the Tour' premieres December 11, followed by 'The Eternal Sunshine Tour' concert film on December 12. The documentary follows the 30 days leading up to the opening of her first tour since 2019, as she simultaneously finished her eighth album 'petal'. Grande executive-produced both films.
articles.body: Grande confirmed on Tuesday, November 24, that fans will get both a behind-the-scenes documentary and a concert film from her Eternal Sunshine Tour, her first tour since 2019. 'The Eternal Sunshine Diaries: The Making of the Tour' premieres on Peacock on December 11, followed by 'The Eternal Sunshine Tour' concert film on December 12, both streaming exclusively on Peacock. The documentary follows Grande in the 30 days leading up to the opening of her sold-out tour, capturing the creative process of finalising the show while she simultaneously prepared to release her eighth album, 'petal'. The tour kicked off in June in Oakland, and its set list included 11 songs from 'Eternal Sunshine', plus selections from 'Positions', 'Dangerous Woman' and 'Thank U, Next', as well as Petal's 'Hate That I Made You Love Me', with more Petal songs added by the end of the run. Peacock describes the tour as a journey 'through the collapse of her reality, a cosmic rebirth, a reconnection with her inner child, and the memories that shaped her', and the concert film as 'a cinematic celebration of healing, connection, and the music that has defined [her] life'. Grande helped oversee both films and holds an executive producer credit on each. She has also said the reaction to her 'Petal' video felt like 'Black Mirror'. The announcement was reported by Rolling Stone on November 24, with Variety reporting the Peacock details.

articles.title: Nick Carter loses bid to dismiss Melissa Schuman sexual battery claim; trial set for May 2027
articles.description: A Los Angeles County judge has rejected Backstreet Boys singer Nick Carter's bid to dismiss a sexual battery claim brought by singer-actress Melissa Schuman, clearing the way for a trial on May 10, 2027. Judge Lisa K. Sepe-Wiesenfeld ruled on November 23 that conflicting evidence over the alleged 2003 assault must be resolved at trial. The ruling turns on California's Assembly Bill 250, the Justice for Survivors of Sexual Assault Act, which took effect January 1 and opens a two-year revival window for otherwise time-barred adult sexual abuse claims.
articles.body: Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Lisa K. Sepe-Wiesenfeld denied Carter's request for summary adjudication on Monday, November 23, finding that conflicting evidence over the alleged assault must be resolved at trial. Schuman, a singer and actress and former member of the pop group Dream, sued Carter in April 2023, alleging he sexually assaulted her at his Santa Monica apartment in 2003, when she was 18 and he was 23. The ruling turns on California's Assembly Bill 250, known as the Justice for Survivors of Sexual Assault Act, which took effect on January 1 and opens a two-year revival window for otherwise time-barred claims of adult sexual abuse against individual perpetrators. Unlike the law in effect when Schuman first sued, the new statute allows lawsuits against individuals without requiring plaintiffs to establish a cover-up or name a business as a defendant. The judge wrote: 'The individual claim against defendant Carter for sexual battery is proper irrespective of the existence of a cover-up. Defendants cannot prevail on summary adjudication merely by attacking the cover-up allegations.' She added: 'There is a conflict in the evidence presented as to whether a sexual assault of plaintiff occurred. Accordingly, a triable issue of material fact is present.' At a November 6 hearing, Carter's lawyer Dale Hayes Jr. argued Schuman's 'only evidence' of a cover-up came from Shannon Ruth, who alleges Carter sexually assaulted her on a tour bus outside the Tacoma Dome in Washington after a show on February 25, 2001. Carter denies the allegations and maintains the relationship was consensual; he previously tried to move the case to Nevada and filed a $2.5 million cross-complaint alleging a conspiracy to defame him. No criminal charges have been filed. Schuman's attorneys, Guinness Costello and Jamie Majerus, praised the decision, saying Schuman will finally have her day in court in May.

articles.title: U2 salute Dolly Parton with 'Torn' duet at first Thanksgiving Eve NFL halftime show
articles.description: U2 headlined the halftime show of the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game on Wednesday night, November 25, performing at SoFi Stadium during the Green Bay Packers-Los Angeles Rams game, streamed live on Netflix. The set included a tribute to the late Dolly Parton, with Bono duetting with her vocals on 'Torn', her final recording, which appears on U2's new album 'Carnaval de Luz'. The band also played 'Sunday Bloody Sunday', 'Where the Streets Have No Name' and 'Pride (In the Name of Love)'.
articles.body: The legendary Irish band headlined the halftime show of the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game on Wednesday night, November 25, as the Green Bay Packers faced the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium, with the game streamed live on Netflix from 8 p.m. ET. At the top of the set, the four bandmates walked to centre field as a choir recited the lyrics of 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For', before Bono launched into 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' over Larry Mullen Jr.'s military-style drum pattern. The mood then changed as U2 paid tribute to the late Dolly Parton, her smiling image splashed on three sails towering over the circular centre stage, with Bono duetting with Parton's vocals on 'Torn', her very last recording, which appears on the band's 16th studio album 'Carnaval de Luz'. The band then played 'Where the Streets Have No Name' and closed with 'Pride (In the Name of Love)', the tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. from their 1984 album 'The Unforgettable Fire'. The performance came 24 years after U2's celebrated Super Bowl XXXVI halftime show in 2002, which also featured the Rams. 'Carnaval de Luz', released November 13, debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on the UK Albums Chart, and the band is marking its 50th anniversary this year. U2's stadium tour, 'The Greatest Show on Earth', launches with a Miami concert in August 2027, its first stadium tour since 2019.

articles.title: ATEEZ score fourth Billboard 200 No. 1 with 'GOLDEN HOUR : Part.6'
articles.description: ATEEZ have earned their fourth No. 1 on the Billboard 200 as 'GOLDEN HOUR : Part.6' debuts atop the chart dated November 28. The 15th mini-album earned 195,000 equivalent album units in the US in the week ending November 19, according to Luminate, including 191,000 in pure album sales. The debut gives ATEEZ 10 consecutive top-10 albums, the most top-10 entries of any group in the 2020s.
articles.body: Billboard announced the chart on November 22, with the ranking dated November 28 and reflecting the tracking week ending November 19. It is ATEEZ's fourth Billboard 200 No. 1, following 'THE WORLD EP.FIN : WILL', 'GOLDEN HOUR : Part.2' and 'GOLDEN HOUR : Part.5', and their second chart-topper of 2026 after Part.5 in July. The debut is overwhelmingly a physical-sales story: of the 195,000 equivalent album units, 191,000 came from traditional album sales, with streaming contributing only about 4,000 units. The five-track EP, released November 13 and led by the title track 'Up', also put ATEEZ on the Hot 100, with 'Up' entering at No. 90. The group now has 10 consecutive top-10 albums on the Billboard 200, the most top-10 entries of any group in the 2020s, and the third-most Billboard 200 No. 1s in K-pop group history, behind Stray Kids with nine and BTS with seven. In South Korea the album sold about 2.05 million copies in its first week, making ATEEZ double million-sellers for the first time since debut, according to the Hanteo Chart. The 195,000 US units are lower than the roughly 228,000 attributed to Part.5 earlier this year, even though both albums reached No. 1. ATEEZ also notched their eighth No. 1 on the Top Album Sales chart with the debut.

articles.title: Karol G's 'BbY WOW' returns to No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200 for a seventh week
articles.description: Karol G's 'BbY WOW', with Judeline and Rusowsky, has returned to No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200 for a seventh nonconsecutive week, and extends its run atop Global Excl. U.S. to eight weeks. The track earned 36.5 million streams worldwide in the November 13-19 tracking week, according to Luminate. Christmas songs are already crowding the top five: Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' climbs to No. 4 and Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' to No. 5.
articles.body: The charts are dated November 28 and were reported by Billboard on November 23, reflecting the November 13-19 tracking week. 'BbY WOW' first reached No. 1 on both global charts in mid-September, and this is its seventh nonconsecutive week atop the Global 200 after Tate McRae's 'Housewife' interrupted its run with four weeks at No. 1. The track earned 36.5 million streams worldwide in the latest tracking week, including 29.8 million outside the United States. Beneath Karol G, Ashe's 'Stop the Wedding!' rises from No. 3 to No. 2 for a new Global 200 peak, while McRae's 'Housewife' slides two spots to No. 3. The Christmas catalog is already crowding the top five: Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' climbs from No. 8 to No. 4 with 28.8 million global streams, and Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' jumps from No. 14 to No. 5 with 26 million. 'Last Christmas' first topped the Global 200 last holiday season, for two weeks, while Carey's 1994 standard has now led the chart for 20 weeks, the most since the list began in 2020. The Global 200 and Global Excl. U.S. rank songs on streaming and sales across more than 200 territories, compiled by Luminate, which reviews and authenticates the data before the charts are finalised. The early arrival of holiday songs in the top five before Thanksgiving is now an annual pattern.

articles.title: U2's 'Carnaval de Luz' debuts at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 and tops three charts
articles.description: U2's new album 'Carnaval de Luz' debuts at No. 4 on the Billboard 200, the band's 14th top 10 on the chart, and opens in the top 10 on seven Billboard charts dated November 28. It tops Top Rock Albums, Vinyl Albums and Indie Store Album Sales, and reaches No. 2 on Top Album Sales, Top Alternative Albums and Top Rock & Alternative Albums. The set earned 49,000 equivalent album units in the US in the week ending November 19, according to Luminate.
articles.body: The album opens in the top 10 on seven Billboard charts dated November 28, including No. 1 on Top Rock Albums, Vinyl Albums and Indie Store Album Sales. It also debuts at No. 2 on Top Album Sales, Top Alternative Albums and Top Rock & Alternative Albums. Of the 49,000 equivalent album units earned in the week ending November 19, album sales account for 42,500, streaming equivalent units for 5,500 (equal to 5.77 million on-demand official streams) and track equivalent units for 1,000. The No. 4 debut is U2's 14th top 10 on the Billboard 200, a run dating back to 'The Joshua Tree', which debuted at No. 7 on April 4, 1987, on its way to nine weeks at No. 1 as the first of the band's eight chart leaders. It is the band's second Billboard 200 top 10 this decade, following 'Songs of Surrender' at No. 5 in 2023. The album also debuted at No. 1 on the Official UK Albums Chart and Australia's ARIA Chart, its 12th UK No. 1. Lead single 'Silencio' marked the group's 45th entry on the Alternative Airplay chart earlier in November, tying Foo Fighters for the most in the chart's history. 'Carnaval de Luz', the band's 16th studio album, was released November 13, and U2 headlined the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL halftime show on November 25. The band is marking its 50th anniversary this year, with a stadium tour launching in Miami in August 2027.

articles.title: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' soundtrack debuts at No. 1 on the Soundtracks chart
articles.description: The soundtrack to 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' debuts at No. 1 on Billboard's Soundtracks chart dated November 28, the franchise's third leader there and its first since 'Catching Fire' in 2013. The set features Noah Kahan, Ella Langley, Kacey Musgraves and Stevie Nicks, plus Jennifer Lawrence returning to sing a new version of 'Deep in the Meadow'. The film is the series' second prequel, set 24 years before the original film.
articles.body: The set debuts at No. 1 on the Soundtracks chart dated November 28, the franchise's third leader on the list and its first since 'The Hunger Games: Catching Fire' in 2013. The earlier No. 1s were 'The Hunger Games: Songs From District 12 and Beyond' in 2012 and 'Catching Fire' in 2013. The new album features Noah Kahan, Ella Langley, Kacey Musgraves and Stevie Nicks, with lead single 'Draw You Out' by Kahan, and Jennifer Lawrence returns to sing a new version of 'Deep in the Meadow', the lullaby Katniss sang to Rue in the original film. Other contributors include The Smashing Pumpkins with 'Black Stars', Lizzy McAlpine, Diji Perez and Hudson Freeman, in a lineup praised for its dark, cinematic atmosphere bridging generations of artists. The soundtrack also debuts at No. 4 on Top Album Sales and No. 13 on the Billboard 200. 'Sunrise on the Reaping' is the second prequel in the film series, with events set 24 years before the first 'Hunger Games' film. The franchise has a tradition of high-profile, artist-driven soundtracks: Lorde curated 'Mockingjay Part 1', and Olivia Rodrigo contributed 'Can't Catch Me Now' to 'The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes'. The chart reflects the November 13-19 tracking week.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' scores her fourth Pop Airplay No. 1
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' has reached No. 1 on Billboard's Pop Airplay chart, her fourth leader there. It is the second No. 1 from her album 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love', following 'Drop Dead'. The album itself held No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for a fifth nonconsecutive week on the chart dated November 21, earning 62,000 equivalent album units.
articles.body: The Pop Airplay chart, dated November 28, measures mainstream top 40 radio in the US and reflects the November 13-19 tracking week. 'Stupid Song' is the second No. 1 from Rodrigo's album 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love', following 'Drop Dead'. The album itself continues its long chart run: it held No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for a fifth nonconsecutive week on the chart dated November 21, earning 62,000 equivalent album units in the tracking week ending November 12. On the latest Billboard 200, dated November 28, the album falls to No. 2 with 62,000 units, down 1%, behind ATEEZ's new No. 1. Lil Baby's 'FRESH' debuted at No. 2 that week with 59,000 units, even though he out-streamed Rodrigo with 56.81 million streams. Morgan Wallen's 'I'm the Problem' holds at No. 3 with just over 49,000 units, while P1Harmony's 'BLOW UP' enters at No. 4 on 45,000 units, including 43,500 album sales, matching the group's best-ever rank. Rodrigo's album has now spent 23 weeks on the Billboard 200. The Pop Airplay No. 1 shows the album's radio legs beyond its streaming strength, keeping Rodrigo at the top of both the albums and radio charts in the same month.

articles.title: Bruno Mars lands third Adult Contemporary No. 1 as Remi Wolf earns her first chart-topper
articles.description: Bruno Mars has scored his third No. 1 on Billboard's Adult Contemporary chart with 'I Just Might', while Remi Wolf earns her first-ever No. 1 on any Billboard chart as 'Bottle' tops Adult Alternative Airplay. Both moves come on the charts dated November 28, reflecting the November 13-19 tracking week. The two milestones show the week's chart spread reaching from established hitmakers to first-time chart-toppers.
articles.body: Both milestones come on Billboard's charts dated November 28, reflecting the November 13-19 tracking week compiled by Luminate. Mars' 'I Just Might' marks his third No. 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart, the radio format for softer mainstream pop, adding to a long career of radio success. The song follows his recent run of high-profile collaborations and solo returns, and its AC success shows its reach beyond streaming and pop radio. Remi Wolf's 'Bottle' tops Adult Alternative Airplay, the Triple A format known for breaking indie and alternative acts, giving the singer-songwriter her first No. 1 on any Billboard chart. For Wolf it is a career milestone, her first time leading a Billboard ranking in any format. The two songs sit at opposite ends of the week's chart story: an established hitmaker consolidating his radio dominance, and a newer artist breaking through for the first time. Both were featured in Billboard's weekly Chart Beat highlights alongside ATEEZ, U2, Ella Langley, Mariah Carey and Wham!, in a week when the charts were dominated by new album debuts and the early arrival of Christmas songs.

articles.title: Jagged Edge's Brandon Casey sued by woman alleging childhood abuse and a stolen hit song
articles.description: Jagged Edge member Brandon Casey is facing a civil lawsuit filed by singer-songwriter Tyliyah Lee, 29, who alleges he sexually assaulted her as a child in the early 2000s and stole a song she wrote. The complaint, obtained by Billboard, alleges five assaults when Lee was aged six to ten, after they met at a Philadelphia community event in 2003. Casey flatly denies the allegations through his lawyer, who calls them baseless and uncorroborated; the claims are unproven and no trial date has been set.
articles.body: Lee, 29, first filed the suit in a Philadelphia county court in September, seeking at least $50,000 in damages for severe emotional distress and substantial depression and anxiety. The complaint alleges she met Casey at a Philadelphia community event in 2003 and that he had nonconsensual sexual intercourse with her on five separate occasions when she was between six and ten years old. Lee, a singer-songwriter, also claims she wrote the 2003 Jagged Edge hit 'Walked Outta Heaven' when she was six, and that Casey took the song after she played it for him without crediting or compensating her, though the lawsuit brings no copyright infringement claim over the song. 'Walked Outta Heaven' reached No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 2 on Billboard's Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart, and Casey is credited as an arranger and lyricist alongside his twin brother Brian Casey, while Bryan-Michael Cox holds the composition credit. Casey's attorneys moved the case to federal court on November 19, and the filing states that Lee demanded a $15 million settlement before suing. Casey's lawyer, Leron Rogers of Fox Rothschild, said in a November 23 statement to Billboard that the singer 'flatly rejects the untrue allegations' and 'will not be pressured by headlines'. A response in the case is reported to be due December 18, and no trial date has been set. The allegations are unproven, and Casey denies each and every allegation of wrongdoing.

articles.title: Jared Kushner's Undisclosed Investment
articles.author: Ariel Sabar
articles.description: An exclusive built on SEC filings: Kushner's firm quietly held a $32 million stake in a U.S. defense contractor while he served as Trump's peace envoy — and disclosed it only two days after the midterms.
articles.body:
The piece opens with Jared Kushner furious at an October 1 CNN investigation suggesting he was profiting from the war in Gaza while serving as a U.S. mediator. His firm, Affinity Partners, was the largest shareholder in Phoenix Financial, an Israeli company whose stakes in nine Israeli defense contractors, worth hundreds of millions of dollars, had all risen as the war boosted demand for their products. Kushner fired back in long online posts, insisting the report was unfair: Affinity's first investment in Phoenix, $129 million in July 2024, came months before Trump was reelected and half a year before Kushner returned to public service as a volunteer peace envoy. He stressed he had no control over Phoenix's investment choices, likening it to the Israeli equivalent of Vanguard or Fidelity, and that neither he nor Affinity directly owned any of the defense contractors.

What Kushner never mentioned was a second, direct holding. Affinity also owned a $32 million stake in a sprawling American defense contractor, bought after Trump's reelection and Kushner's return to public service but not disclosed until November 5, two days after the midterm elections, when Affinity belatedly amended a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, not previously reported, showed Affinity had acquired 689,411 shares in Arxis, a Connecticut-based company making mission-critical components for F-35 fighter jets, Navy destroyers, nuclear submarines and anti-missile systems, most of them deployed in the Middle East or Russia-Ukraine theaters where Kushner has acted as a key negotiator.

Arxis brings together more than 30 aerospace and defense companies under one umbrella and went public in April. Its filings stress dependence on the U.S. government for revenue, approvals, export controls and security clearances, and its prospectus noted the administration was prioritizing high-tech platforms Arxis supports, from the F-35 to DDG-51 destroyers, Virginia-class submarines and next-generation missile-warning satellites. Of its $1.6 billion in revenue last year, about 47 percent came from defense and space spending, and the company projected U.S. military spending would reach $1 trillion in the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026, driven by multi-theater conflicts and rising geopolitical tensions. Arxis lost money in 2023 and 2024 but turned profitable in 2025, the year Trump returned to office, and its stock has risen about 60 percent since going public.

Under SEC rules, investment managers holding more than $100 million in certain public securities must disclose them within 45 days of each quarter. Yet when Affinity filed its required Form 13F for the second quarter of 2026 in mid-August, it mentioned no Arxis shares at all, disclosing only $565 million of stock in a building-supplies company called QXO. Not until November 5, nearly three months later, did Affinity amend the form, declaring the Arxis investment an omission without explanation. Neither Kushner nor Affinity's communications staff replied to repeated requests for comment.

The article then widens the lens. Kushner, Trump's billionaire son-in-law, has faced accusations for a decade of mixing private and public business, first by failing to fully divest from his family's real-estate empire and now as owner of Affinity, founded in 2021. He raised as much as $6 billion for the firm largely from sovereign-wealth funds in the same Gulf states he now deals with as a peace negotiator, and invested it in ventures including a classifieds company in the United Arab Emirates, a Brazilian fast-food chain and the video-game maker Electronic Arts. Arxis appears to be its first direct defense investment, a major departure, ripe with potential conflicts: his father-in-law holds broad power over military spending, while Kushner mediates conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza whose duration and outcomes bear directly on the defense industry. Had the stake been disclosed before the election, it would have bolstered the CNN report, a New Yorker article from September and a late-October book claiming Kushner had access to secret bank accounts funded by Gulf rulers, a claim he denies, and undercut his unusually voluble public denials. The pattern appears to be continuing: on November 12, a week after Affinity reported its Arxis stake, another company announced Kushner's firm as a new investor, Q-Ctrl, which sells navigation technology sought by the U.S. military because it cannot be jammed or spoofed like GPS. Last year Q-Ctrl won a $24.4 million contract from DARPA and a joint award with Lockheed Martin from the Defense Innovation Unit. Before founding Affinity, Kushner had no substantive private-equity experience, raising the question of why nearly all its money comes from Gulf royals with an existential stake in his diplomacy. The article closes with the question he now faces: why would a man working for peace be seeking to profit from war?

articles.title: Inside an AI prophet's secretive visions for humanity's future
articles.author: Nitasha Tiku
articles.description: Published days after Anthropic's record IPO, this profile asks how a CEO who warns AI could end civilization can also run a $2 trillion public company — and shows the quasi-religious culture inside it.
articles.body:
The profile opens on a contradiction. Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive of Anthropic, has spent years warning that artificial intelligence could end or permanently stunt human civilization, and this week the company he leads became one of the most valuable corporations on Earth. Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq on November 19 in what multiple outlets describe as the largest initial public offering in history. Shares opened at $111.50, 34 percent above the $83 IPO price, and the company's market value briefly blew past $2 trillion; the offering of roughly 980 million shares raised about $81 billion, eclipsing SpaceX's June listing. At the opening bell Amodei struck a reassuring note, saying the listing put the company in a stronger financial position and only strengthened its resolve to do the right thing, and that Anthropic would pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as necessary to have confidence they are safe and will remain under human control.

The financial picture behind the debut is more precarious than it looked. Anthropic carries $6.2 billion in debt and is unprofitable under standard accounting rules, and it has signed leases and deals requiring about $900 billion in computing and infrastructure spending, including $70 billion in the next 12 months. The Post's portrait describes a leader who governs through essays, long Slack memos and twice-monthly all-hands talks jokingly called Dario Vision Quests. Inside the company, staff known as Ants treat several propositions as self-evident: that AI superseding humans is inevitable, that the United States must limit China's AI development, and that Claude, the company's chatbot, might be conscious. Anthropic has invited more than a dozen academics, think-tank fellows and media figures to two-day briefings at its San Francisco headquarters, held under the Chatham House Rule, on how society should navigate powerful AI; guests were asked to read an Amodei essay and the 23,000-word constitution guiding Claude. One attendee, NYU economist Arpit Gupta, told the Post the staff felt the public discourse was failing to prepare society for a transformative event.

The convictions run deep. A previously unreported 2022 internal memo, surfaced through court records, estimated a 20 to 30 percent chance that AGI would lead to the destruction or permanent stunting of humanity and called capable AI more powerful and dangerous than nuclear weapons. One former colleague recalled that Amodei used offline, air-gapped laptops and printers for sensitive AI essays, fearing they amounted to an infohazard. Hiring reflects the same intensity: the Post describes a culture interview even for back-office roles, and one hiring manager texted an unsuccessful candidate that it was a bit of an are you ready for the cult interview. The company also ran an internal investigation after Wired reported that Amodei had acknowledged in a Slack message that accepting Middle East state funding was likely to enrich dictators; in that 2025 memo he weighed principle against capital, writing that no bad person should ever benefit from our success was a difficult principle to run a business on. A leaker was later fired, an incident not previously reported. Former employees describe a workforce convinced of its own righteousness, with one telling the Post that the prevailing feeling was that staff would put on their capes and be the responsible ones, accruing great power precisely because they were doing it responsibly.

The profile lands amid a broader reckoning over AI risk. In September, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon publicly resigned, warning that AI could cause human extinction by 2030, a claim echoed by colleagues inside the company; Evan Hubinger, a lead in Anthropic's alignment division, wrote that staff earnestly believed AI could kill all humans. Days later Amodei published an essay, We Must Pace the Frontier, calling for the industry to slow down, drawing rare endorsements from rivals Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk. Yet Amodei publicly downplayed the doomsday framing, telling CNN he is not a doomer and that there is some chance things go wrong but it is not all that high. That gap between internal alarm and public reassurance is the story's central fault line. Geoffrey Irving, a former OpenAI colleague, told the Post that Amodei is just another AI company CEO trapped in this horrible race. Amodei's warnings have also made him enemies in Silicon Valley: the Times reported that Anthropic and OpenAI lobbied the White House to prevent some AI models from being developed and widely shared, prompting Microsoft and then-Nvidia chief Jensen Huang to rally two dozen companies behind a letter defending open models; Amodei refused to sign. The timing could hardly be more fraught: Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains a day after Anthropic's debut amid an AI sell-off, and voters in dozens of local ballot measures this month rejected data centers, with newly elected Democratic governors in Texas and Georgia campaigning on restricting them. For Amodei, the question is whether a publicly traded, profit-driven giant can remain faithful to a mission of protecting humanity, or whether, as his own 2022 memo feared, the incentives of the market will erode it. The prophet has his capital; whether he keeps his congregation is another matter.

articles.title: After a Record Loss, Leopold Aschenbrenner Is Still Betting Everything on A.I.
articles.author: Stephen Witt
articles.description: The 25-year-old who turned a viral AI essay into a $45 billion fund, blew up $30 billion in a month, got married the next day — and still insists 2027 is the last normal year. A remarkable character study of the AI boom's truest believer.
articles.body:
Leopold Aschenbrenner, the twenty-five-year-old manager of Situational Awareness LP, a San Francisco hedge fund, entered Columbia University at fifteen, wrote a forty-four-page economics paper at seventeen that leading figures considered Ph.D.-quality work, and graduated at nineteen as valedictorian. From late 2024 to mid-2026 his fund reported returns of more than a thousand percent, mostly through investments in the AI industry. Then, this summer, it blew up, suffering one of the largest trading losses in American stock-market history, with about two-thirds of its value wiped out, though earlier gains kept its returns positive for the year.

Aschenbrenner's big idea is that the world has not yet grasped the implications of the AI revolution. Next year, calendar year 2027, we will see AI accelerate between two and five times faster than anything we have seen so far, he told the writer, adding that next year is the last year that anything in modern life still feels a little normal. He laid out the thesis in 2024 in a 165-page essay, Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, predicting that by 2027 spending on AI infrastructure would rival the entire U.S. defense budget, that AI companies would be targeted by Chinese spies, that traditional software firms would struggle as AI automated their work, and that AI would outperform even Ph.D.s at intellectual tasks. All of that has occurred, and the Leopold trade, buying shares in data-center suppliers and betting against vulnerable software stocks, has been profitable. His most striking prediction has not yet come to pass: that AI itself will automate AI research, leading to an explosion in superintelligence. That may be why, even while being forced to liquidate most of his holdings this summer, he fought to hold on to the fund's most prized asset, an early stake in Anthropic, whose IPO last week valued the company at about $1.5 trillion.

The path to the fund ran through Silicon Valley's intellectual fringes, including effective-altruism circles and Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute, where he met his future wife Avital Balwit. He worked for the philanthropic-investment arm of FTX, resigning with Balwit on November 11, 2022, the day it filed for bankruptcy, then joined OpenAI's superalignment team of about twenty people. Worried OpenAI was becoming a target for Chinese espionage, he sent a memo to board members in late 2023 over Sam Altman's head, and was fired in April 2024, with OpenAI saying he had leaked confidential information; he maintains the firing was retaliation. Undeterred, he raised money for what he described as a think tank inside a hedge fund, backed by investors including Stripe founders Patrick and John Collison. The fund launched in late 2024 with more than a hundred million dollars, bought power companies and memory-chip makers while betting against software vendors like Adobe, and treated the early-2025 DeepSeek panic as a buying opportunity. He also invested in Anthropic, whose March 2025 round valued it at about sixty billion dollars; his wife had become chief of staff to CEO Dario Amodei. By mid-2026 the fund had about forty billion dollars under management, and with leverage was pushing around a hundred billion.

The blowup came fast. Data centers were buying up the flash-memory supply, and Sandisk's stock rose eightfold; Situational Awareness held more than five billion dollars of Sandisk and was reporting returns above four hundred percent for the first part of the year. By July, investors worried a flash-memory shortage would be followed by a glut, and Sandisk began to fall. Aschenbrenner treated the dip as a buying opportunity, but this time prices did not recover, while software stocks including Accenture proved unexpectedly resilient. On July 24 he wrote investors, who by then included the University of Virginia's endowment, arguing conditions offered some of the best opportunities he had seen in more than a year. Instead, brokers began issuing margin calls. On July 29, investor David Mann received a call in a cab to LaGuardia: Situational Awareness was offering a discounted stake in Anthropic and needed the deal done overnight. A consortium led by Greenoaks and Sequoia worked overnight to structure the deal, but shortly before signing Aschenbrenner reversed course and kept the Anthropic stake, selling the bulk of his public-stock portfolio to Ken Griffin's Citadel at a ten-percent discount instead. The fund told investors it had lost an estimated thirty billion dollars in July, the single biggest drawdown in hedge-fund history. The next day, August 1, Aschenbrenner got married.

A reconstruction by Rich Falk-Wallace, a former Citadel portfolio manager, found Aschenbrenner was an excellent stock picker who nailed which part of the supply chain the narrative would hit next, but took on more risk than any hedge fund Falk-Wallace had ever seen: where a typical fund runs at about five percent implied volatility and a very aggressive one at thirty, Situational Awareness was somewhere close to a hundred percent, and its hardware and software trades were inversely correlated, so if one side failed the other probably would too. Despite the wipeout, the fund remains profitable for most backers and still holds more than ten billion dollars. Aschenbrenner has cut back on leverage but kept betting on Sandisk, whose share price is now lower than when he was forced to sell it. Nvidia has fallen more than thirty percent from its peak after CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, while Accenture posted record earnings in October. GDP growth looks set to come in around three percent rather than the ten percent he predicted, unemployment is stable at about four percent, and a survey found workers using AI saved only about two percent of their time. Aschenbrenner is unmoved: the models have started doing a meaningful share of the research that makes the next models, he wrote, and with it comes a drastic acceleration in AI progress. Even the skeptical Dwarkesh Patel has come around, conceding Leopold was much more foresighted on timelines than he was. Aschenbrenner showed the writer a chart of actual AI capabilities versus analyst projections: every year since 2022, analysts expected AI to plateau, and every year it kept progressing, while the goalposts moved. He closed with the Anthropic employees he admires: wonderful people, noble and earnest, with great minds, and all of them believe that in a few years they will be replaced. In ten years, are people gonna ask me what to invest in, he asked. No. They're gonna ask an AI.

articles.title: The Kings of Cocaine Are Masters of Stealth
articles.author: Ed Caesar
articles.description: A gripping reported feature from inside Brazil's P.C.C. — a gang with a constitution, its own courts, and a leader ruling from a maximum-security cell — and why calling it a terrorist group may make everything worse.
articles.body:
The piece opens inside the Penitenciária Federal de Brasília, one of five federal maximum-security prisons in Brazil. Completed in 2018, it sits on scrubland nine miles outside the capital. Its perimeter wall is thirty feet high and fifty feet belowground. Cells measure sixty-five square feet, with poured-concrete furniture. There are no televisions, radios, clocks or newspapers. Inmates get two hours outside their cells each day. The most notable prisoner is Marcos Willians Herbas Camacho, known as Marcola. Since the early 2000s, experts say, the fifty-eight-year-old has led Latin America's largest criminal organization, Primeiro Comando da Capital, the P.C.C. It claims more than forty thousand initiated brothers and sixty thousand associates, and dominates the cocaine traffic from Brazil to Europe. Marcola has been in prison throughout his leadership. Wiretaps published in September show him still issuing coded orders through prison air vents.

In June, the Trump Administration designated the P.C.C. a foreign terrorist organization. The rationale was hazy, invoking narco-terrorists flooding American streets. Yet the P.C.C.'s drugs rarely reach the United States, where cocaine comes mostly from Mexican traffickers. Its ideology scarcely resembles a terrorist agenda. What it wants is not terror but control. Where it dominates, homicides have become comparatively rare. São Paulo's murder rate spiked at fifty-two per hundred thousand in the late nineties. It is now about five, a ninety-percent drop, similar to Austin, Texas. As political scientist Bruno Paes Manso put it, they are not a cartel. They are the governors of crime, the national development bank of crime. They establish rules.

The gang was born from a massacre. On October 2, 1992, a dispute in Block 9 of the Carandiru prison in São Paulo spiraled into rebellion. More than seven thousand men were crowded onto a campus built for three thousand. Military police fired more than three thousand rounds in twenty minutes, killing a hundred and eleven prisoners. The P.C.C. was founded in August 1993 as a kind of prisoners' union by men transferred from Carandiru to a prison in Taubaté. It adopted the yin-yang symbol and imposed a strict legal framework codified in a written estatuto, or constitution, drafted with advice from two Italian mobsters. The document clamped down on sexual assault and banned robbery, rape and extortion within the system.

The other central figure is Lincoln Gakiya, a fifty-nine-year-old public prosecutor with about eighty heavily armed military-police officers protecting him around the clock. He told the writer, I feel like I'm in jail. He became the P.C.C.'s nemesis almost by accident. A low-ranking prosecutor until 2005, he ordered a gang leader directing drug sales from inside a prison into solitary confinement. The leader ordered a hit; Gakiya got advance warning and fled. In 2006, when some seven hundred members were transferred to his district, Marcola coordinated riots in about seventy state prisons. Gunmen attacked police, killing more than forty officers and guards in one May weekend. Gakiya has since prosecuted many senior figures and recently secured two more convictions adding more than forty years to Marcola's sentence. He explained the gang's structure: members pursue their own enterprises freely as long as they use the P.C.C.'s supply chains, with divisions handling finance, internal justice, prisoner welfare and trafficking. Asked how much control Marcola could exert from prison, Gakiya said the processes he established let the group flourish without daily instructions: it's almost like Coca-Cola. Crackdowns may even have backfired, making the group, in Nassim Nicholas Taleb's term, antifragile.

Most profits now come from Europe's appetite for cocaine: the gang can buy a kilogram from an Andean supplier for as little as fifteen hundred dollars and sell it to a European crime group for more than thirty thousand. The main exit point is the port of Santos, which Gakiya says is completely controlled by the P.C.C. A customs official showed the writer cameras, sensors, drones and scanners, and a dog named Nutella who found eight hundred pounds of cocaine hidden among coffee sacks. Cocaine is only one business: the gang earns five-hundred-percent profit smuggling cigarettes from Paraguay, profits from generic semaglutide weight-loss drugs made in Ciudad del Este, and was found adulterating gas with methanol at more than a thousand gas stations and laundering billions through fintech firms. The gang also runs its own courts, and a former member described an internal trial that chose expulsion and repayment over death. Killing is bad for business because it attracts the police, and these courts partly explain São Paulo's murder decline, a Pax Mafiosa.

Before the terrorist designation, Gakiya told officials in Secretary of State Marco Rubio's office that the P.C.C. was a big criminal company, a mafia, with a lot of guns, but no politics or ideological purpose. His appraisal was ignored. Jason Blazakis, who ran the U.S. Office of Counterterrorism Finance and Designations from 2008 to 2018, called the rationale worrisome: his office never gave the terrorist label to a group whose primary purpose was criminal, because once you start designating cartels, where do you stop? President Lula condemned the implication that it gave the U.S. license to intervene inside Brazilian territory, saying, We do not accept being treated like little boys. The piece closes through Thomas Hobbes's Leviathan: criminals presented with chaos in Brazil's prison system chose to create their own order. The final scene is a visit to a Paraguayan prison wing controlled by the P.C.C., where the wing's boss, who called himself Miguel, a member since the gang's founding in 1993, explained he had already paid half a bribe to secure his release. We are not terrorists, one of the brothers insisted. We are organized criminals. Miguel said he had put much of the money he made back into poor communities. We were Robin Hoods, he said. We stole and gave it away. Asked what he would do when freed, he answered: Rob banks in Brazil. I don't know how to do anything else.

articles.title: Mary Gauthier Wants to Help You Heal
articles.author: Sarah Larson
articles.description: A warm, funny Chelsea Hotel encounter with the 64-year-old Nashville songwriter ahead of her eleventh album — Springsteen, Patti Smith, Dylan, sobriety, and healing through song.
articles.body:
On a recent trip to New York, shortly before the release of her eleventh studio album, Reckoning, the Nashville-based singer-songwriter Mary Gauthier paid a visit to a longtime inspiration, the Chelsea Hotel, and when she got there she befriended the doorman. I told him I loved his crazy hair, and he said, I love your overalls, she said, reclining on a chaise in the lobby. Gauthier, sixty-four, has spiky gray hair and wore pink-tinted glasses, a pink shirt, a neckerchief, and faded denim overalls with appliquéd strawberries the size of grapefruit. I think this is kind of my uniform now, she said. I'm done wearing clothes that make my body hurt. This works on airplanes, it's got pockets so big you don't even know if your cellphone is in it, it's a good conversation starter, little kids love it. The doorman, a fan, offered to give her a hotel tour. Crazy, right? she said. I operate kind of under the radar, so when someone is aware of my songs I'm very honored. She's honored fairly often: I've got a Forrest Gump quality about me, she said. I walk into the most ridiculous situations. Examples: Robert Plant, at a red-carpet London movie première, putting his arm around me and saying, I don't know about all of this, I like what you're doing; Nanci Griffith giving Gauthier her guitar at a Nashville houseparty, after she'd borrowed it to play a song; and her hero Bob Dylan, years ago, playing her standout I Drink on his radio show. Extraordinarily validating, she said. You know, if Bob likes you, you might want to consider trying to like yourself.

Gauthier started life in a Catholic orphanage, born a bastard child in New Orleans to a woman I've never seen, as she sings in Goodbye, and after being adopted felt like a misfit at home in Baton Rouge, with volatile parents. She went to drug rehab at age fifteen, when she also encountered Dylan's songs. Music was a salvation: later, underage at gay bars, we'd clear the dance floor and make them put on Patti Smith, she said. Horses was a life jacket in an ocean of Baton Rouge. We'd thrash about and scream all the words. Horses was an important part of knowing there's a bigger world out there. Patti did that for a lot of kids. Such kids went to New York, and to the Chelsea, the landing ground for outsiders, Gauthier said. It's part of all our hero stories, right? She began writing songs after she got sober, in 1990, following a fateful drunk-driving arrest in Boston, where she was running a Cajun restaurant. She recalls the process in her memoir, Saved by a Song, from 2021.

Reckoning, her new album, was heavily influenced by Bruce Springsteen's Nebraska: a stripped-down sound of voice, guitar and harmonica, with no intrusion of production and largesse, a collection of stories that hold together as a body of work, and a through line to Flannery O'Connor, whose fiction Springsteen was deep-diving in right before he was writing Nebraska. Gauthier has visited O'Connor's house in Milledgeville, Georgia. O'Connor was like a chainsaw, cutting down hypocrisy, cutting down ignorance, she said. She was just a ramrod. In her book, Gauthier talks about healing through songwriting, and about helping mentees, including wounded veterans, do so, too. I'm in awe of the human ability to make meaning out of suffering, she said. I'm real glad I have a guitar and I can make music with it and fight against that as an artist. Which is probably what people have been doing in this building for a long, long time.

Before Gauthier left, the doorman-historian, in a black suit and tinted glasses with Richard Hell hair, squired her around upstairs, noting rooms of interest, where Dylan Thomas fell into a coma, where Dylan wrote parts of Blonde on Blonde, where Madonna shot Sex, and discussing others, the Sid and Nancy room, the Janis and Leonard room, the Patti and Robert room. Recently the hotel's management proposed putting up site-specific notable-guest photos. They wanted a list of where people lived, he said. I was, like, I don't know, man, it seems a little bohemian Cracker Barrel. He unlocked the door to 2-W, which featured Art Deco stained glass, and led Gauthier to a street-facing balcony, just beneath the famous neon sign. Primo selfie territory! he said. Gauthier beamed and took some primo snapshots.

articles.title: Long Live the Chip King
articles.author: Brady Brickner-Wood
articles.description: The sharpest, funniest account of the Nvidia saga: Trump posting an AI image of a blood-splattered Jensen Huang in his own Butler pose — and what it reveals about whose interests the White House now serves.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's Truth Social account is many things: a disturbing stream of consciousness, a nationwide embarrassment, a place where professionalism and discretion, and truth, generally go to die. But often the feed is a gallery of self-portraits, many of them AI-generated: Trump as a pontiff; Trump as a king; Trump as a king and a fighter pilot, dumping sewage on protesters, in a video set to Danger Zone by Kenny Loggins. In this context, the image Trump posted on Monday, of a blood-splattered Jensen Huang, Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, victoriously hoisting a brassiere, might barely even register. And yet the photo is an anomaly, not because it's so vulgar, this is the same account that once shared a clip of the Obamas as apes, but because it is glorifying someone who is not Donald Trump. If anything, the photo, a play on the iconic picture taken of Trump after he was nearly assassinated at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, is a strange self-own, a diminishment of the event that helped Trump reclaim the Presidency, and a reminder of whose interests it is that the White House now serves.

In the picture, seemingly made with AI and posted without a caption, Trump has been replaced by Huang, and the American flag by a black-and-green Nvidia flag. Huang is raising his fist, just as Trump did, but his fingers are clasped around a red underwire bra, red because bras are seemingly always red in the male imagination but also presumably because Huang's initial downfall was prompted by allegations that he was sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy. Not long after Nvidia announced Huang's return, an about-face that came just eleven days after his resignation, Trump took credit for the company's decision to bring him back. I convinced them, he told CNBC in a hallucinatory, nearly hour-long phone interview. I made the deal. He noted, We have to protect our geniuses, and he's certainly a genius. It is ironic, to say the least, that one of the most anti-science Presidents in recent memory, one who has gutted university funding and waged war against individual scientists such as Anthony Fauci, is now claiming that he wants to protect geniuses. But it is true that Trump has consistently worked to protect Jensen Huang.

The timeline runs like this. On November 8, Nvidia, the world's biggest chip company, announced that it was opening an investigation into Huang, who had been romantically involved with a woman determined by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. China has denied that the woman, Alice Huang, is a spy, but the Times recently reported that she kept in contact with an official of China's top spy agency for more than a year during her relationship with the Nvidia CEO. Trump was quick to describe Huang as an honorable guy who probably has an excuse for it. After talking to Huang, Trump explained, He said, I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really believe him. Trump urged Huang not to step down, but when Huang stepped down anyway, on November 12, following reports of two more alleged extramarital affairs with non-spies, both of whom worked under him at Nvidia, Trump briefly pivoted to championing another genius, suggesting former Apple CEO Tim Cook, a man Trump once referred to as Tim Apple, take Huang's place. A Legend replaces a Legend! Trump wrote on Truth Social. The markets weren't as optimistic; the company's stock price dropped more than sixteen percent. Suddenly Trump was on Fox News saying that we have to take care of our geniuses, because we don't have that many of them. On Monday, CNBC asked Trump whether the stock-market losses had prompted his intervention. Trump replied, Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was, you know, he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me. After Nvidia's board reinstated Huang, citing input from senior levels of the United States government, the company's shares surged more than thirty percent.

Trump's obsession with the stock market isn't new, although it has likely been amplified by recent events. The President, reeling from his party's sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, a nationwide repudiation of his Administration's policies, which have exacerbated the affordability crisis, appears determined to avoid a stock-market collapse and an AI-bubble burst, outcomes that would further tank his standing in the final years of his Presidency. Perhaps even more significant are Trump's personal financial ties with Nvidia. A Washington Post investigation found that the President's holdings in the company ballooned to as much as sixty-two million dollars' worth of stock before Huang's scandals became public, with the value of those holdings appreciating amid a series of policy decisions and relaxing of restrictions that benefitted Nvidia's bottom line. Huang has seemingly become one of Trump's closest corporate allies not through a mutual quest to enhance American infrastructure, but through their overlapping personal and financial interests. Genius recognizes genius. Alice Huang isn't just thought to have been a spy for the Chinese government; during her relationship with Jensen Huang, she also worked for the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia chips, which is alleged to have helped Chinese customers circumvent U.S. export controls. Megaspeed is the subject of a U.S. Justice Department probe; Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

In recent months, however, Trump's antagonistic posture toward China has softened. He's been bragging about his outstanding relationship with Xi, and dismissing concerns about Chinese espionage. Trump took a similar tack in his CNBC interview on Monday, arguing that it didn't matter if Alice Huang was in touch with China's Ministry of State Security, since Trump himself was in contact with the agency, too. Pointing to his recent summit with Xi in Shenzhen, Trump said, laughing, I'm involved also if you really get down to it, right? As if a diplomatic meeting between two heads of state were at all comparable to sleeping with a potential spy. Trump even rejected the claim that Alice Huang was an intelligence operative: As far as the woman is concerned: every time you have a Chinese woman that's good-looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy, he told CNBC. He claimed that Huang had been exonerated and did absolutely nothing wrong, language similar to what the President once used to describe his own conduct after the Mueller investigation. Huang's affair, he said, had become a big headline only because of the extramarital indiscretion. Sex sells, fellas, the President said, with the confidence of a man speaking from experience. He predicted that, ultimately, the scandal would be a net positive for Jensen Huang and for Nvidia. As clips from Trump's call circulated on social media on Monday, memes and AI-generated videos flooded the internet, both satirizing and celebrating Huang's triumphant return. In one recurring bit, AI-generated clips recast Huang as Michael Jordan hugging an NBA Finals trophy, evoking a famous photograph of Jordan celebrating his first championship win in 1991, two years before he briefly retired and then returned to play. It was Musk who planted the seed for the Jordan comparison, saying last week that ousting Huang from Nvidia was akin to kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you're on a winning streak. Perhaps that's the kind of future that Trump envisions for Huang.

articles.title: Consortium led by US billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil's foreign assets
articles.description: A consortium led by US billionaire Todd Boehly has agreed to buy Lukoil's foreign assets, Meduza reported. The group includes the US Development Finance Corporation, investment bank Xtellus Partners and a UAE-registered company, with the US government set to take a stake. It would be one of the biggest sales of Russian corporate assets abroad since 2022.
articles.body: A consortium headed by American billionaire Todd Boehly, co-owner of Chelsea football club, has signed an agreement to acquire the foreign assets of Russian oil giant Lukoil, Meduza reported on November 25. Alongside Boehly, the consortium includes the US Development Finance Corporation, American investment bank Xtellus Partners and Catena Investment Holding, a company registered in the United Arab Emirates. The US government itself is set to receive a stake in the deal. Lukoil, one of Russia's largest oil producers, has been under Western sanctions since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and its overseas assets — refineries, petrol stations and trading operations across Europe and beyond — have been a persistent headache for both the company and Western governments. The sale would be one of the largest divestments of Russian corporate assets since 2022, effectively transferring a major slice of Russia's global oil business into Western-aligned hands. It also shows how sanctions are reshaping ownership of Russian energy assets abroad, with politically connected American investors now stepping in where European buyers hesitated.

articles.title: Von der Leyen: EU will join next round of talks with Russia on Ukraine — but only if Moscow agrees to a winter energy ceasefire and a Black Sea truce
articles.description: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced that Europe will join the next round of negotiations with Russia on Ukraine, and said the EU will only open talks with Moscow if Russia agrees to a winter ceasefire on energy infrastructure and a Black Sea truce. She said Brussels will judge Russia 'by its actions, not just by its words'. Moscow dismissed the statement as 'megaphone diplomacy'.
articles.body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament in Strasbourg on November 25 that Europe will take part in the next round of negotiations with Russia on Ukraine, and set out the conditions for the EU to open talks with Moscow itself.
