Independent artists, meanwhile, face a landscape where a viral clip can do more for a song than a full marketing campaign. The report lands as TikTok continues to expand its own music tools, including its in-app streaming service in some markets. Whether the 94% figure holds in 2026 will be watched closely, but the direction of travel is clear: virality on TikTok is now the default route to the world's biggest chart.

articles.title: NetEase Cloud Music's Q3 revenues fell 0.9% YoY to $290m after subscription revenues grew 5.3% in H1
articles.description: NetEase Cloud Music's revenues slipped 0.9% year on year to around $290 million in the third quarter, even though the Chinese streamer re-signed licensing deals with all three major labels this year. Subscription revenue growth has slowed to roughly a third of its pace a year earlier. The slowdown shows how hard it is to keep growing paid music subscriptions in China's crowded, price-sensitive market.
articles.body: NetEase Cloud Music reported third-quarter revenues of around $290 million, down 0.9% year on year, in a softer set of results for China's second-biggest music streamer. The company re-signed licensing agreements with all three major labels this year, securing its catalogue, but that has not translated into faster growth. Subscription revenue growth has slowed to roughly a third of the pace it managed a year earlier, after rising 5.3% in the first half. The figures point to a maturing Chinese streaming market, where competition with Tencent Music is intense and users are reluctant to pay more for subscriptions. NetEase has leaned on social and community features, live streaming and its indie artist ecosystem to differentiate itself, but monetising those features at scale remains a challenge. The results will be watched by the majors, for whom China is a long-term growth bet that has yet to deliver streaming economics comparable to the West. For now, NetEase's story is one of a solid but slowing business in a market where the easy subscriber growth has already been won.

articles.title: UMG and Sony withdraw DistroKid subpoena motion in Suno case after distributor produces AI-detection documents
articles.description: Universal Music Group and Sony Music have withdrawn their motion to subpoena DistroKid in their copyright case against AI music generator Suno, after the distributor handed over documents about how it detects AI-generated tracks. The labels had sought data on how many DistroKid tracks were flagged as AI-generated, how many were attributed to Suno, and what they earned. The withdrawal narrows one front of the labels' wider legal campaign against AI training on copyrighted music.
articles.body: Universal Music Group and Sony Music have withdrawn their motion to force distributor DistroKid to hand over documents in their copyright infringement case against AI music company Suno. The labels had sought data on how many tracks distributed by DistroKid were flagged as AI-generated, how many of those were attributed to Suno, and how much money they earned. DistroKid has now produced AI-detection documents, prompting the labels to drop the subpoena request. The episode is a side battle in the majors' much larger fight with Suno and fellow AI generator Udio, whom they accuse of training models on copyrighted recordings without permission. The data the labels wanted would have helped quantify how much AI-generated music is already flowing through distribution pipelines and earning royalties. DistroKid sits in the middle of that flow as one of the largest distributors for independent artists, making its detection practices a key piece of evidence. The withdrawal does not end the main Suno case, which remains one of the most consequential copyright fights in music. But it shows the labels are willing to de-escalate procedural skirmishes once they get the information they need, keeping the focus on the core question of whether AI training on copyrighted music is infringement.

articles.title: Switzerland's MusicBird secures up to $200M revolving credit facility arranged by Truist and Fifth Third
articles.description: Swiss music-rights company MusicBird has secured a revolving credit facility of up to $200 million, arranged by Truist and Fifth Third. The company says the new financing will help it scale its portfolio of music rights. The deal is the latest sign that debt markets remain open to music-catalogue buyers even as interest rates stay high.
articles.body: Switzerland's MusicBird has secured a revolving credit facility of up to $200 million, arranged by Truist and Fifth Third, in a deal that underlines continued lender appetite for music rights. MusicBird says the new financing will help it scale its portfolio, giving it firepower to acquire more catalogues and royalty streams. Revolving credit facilities have become a standard tool for music-rights companies, letting them draw down funds for acquisitions and repay as royalties come in. The involvement of two major US banks is notable: it suggests institutional lenders still view music royalties as a relatively stable, uncorrelated asset class, despite higher interest rates and a cooling in some parts of the catalogue market. MusicBird is a newer entrant compared with giants like Hipgnosis and Concord, but the size of the facility signals serious ambitions. The deal also reflects a broader trend of European music companies tapping US debt markets to fund growth. For artists and rights-holders considering a sale, the message is that buyers still have access to capital, even if the frothy valuations of a few years ago have moderated.

articles.title: Live experiences platform Speakeasy, backed by Yamaha's music fund, raises $18.8M Series A
articles.description: Speakeasy, a platform for live experiences backed by Yamaha's music fund, has raised an $18.8 million Series A, bringing its total funding to about $27 million. The company builds tools around in-person music and cultural experiences. The raise shows investors still see room for new live-experience platforms even as the post-pandemic live boom matures.
articles.body: Live experiences platform Speakeasy has raised an $18.8 million Series A round, bringing its total funding to approximately $27 million. The company is backed by Yamaha's music fund, a notable vote of confidence from one of the music industry's biggest instrument and technology companies. Speakeasy operates in the live-experiences space, building products around in-person music and cultural events at a time when audiences are spending heavily on going out. The funding comes as the live sector digests a huge post-pandemic boom and looks for the next wave of growth, including better discovery, ticketing and fan-experience tools. Yamaha's involvement is interesting because it connects an instrument maker with the live-experience economy, a pairing that could open distribution and partnership routes. For a startup, $18.8 million is a substantial Series A and suggests investors believe there is still whitespace in how fans find and attend live events. The challenge for Speakeasy will be converting that capital into a durable position against entrenched ticketing and event platforms.

articles.title: $11M-backed AI startup Sonilo, founded by TikTok veterans, inks licensing deal with Symphonic to train its model on opted-in indie recordings
articles.description: Sonilo, an AI music startup founded by TikTok veterans and backed with $11 million, has signed a licensing deal with distributor Symphonic to train its AI model on recordings from independent artists and labels — but only those that opt in. The deal is a rare example of a licensed, consent-based approach to AI music training, in contrast to the unlicensed training alleged in the Suno and Udio lawsuits. It could become a template for how AI companies and the indie sector work together.
articles.body: AI music startup Sonilo, founded by TikTok veterans and backed with $11 million, has signed a licensing deal with Symphonic that allows it to train its AI model on recordings from the distributor's independent artists and labels — but only those that choose to opt in. The agreement is a deliberate contrast to the approach taken by Suno and Udio, which the major labels accuse of training on copyrighted music without permission. By building an opt-in catalogue, Sonilo is betting that consent-based training can be both legally safe and commercially viable, and that indie artists will participate if they are paid and credited. Symphonic, which distributes music for a large roster of independent labels, gains a new revenue stream for its artists and a stake in shaping how AI uses their work. The deal also reflects the growing split in the AI music world between companies seeking licences and those fighting lawsuits. For the indie sector, the opt-in model offers a way to benefit from AI rather than simply being its raw material. Whether enough artists opt in to make Sonilo's model competitive remains an open question, but the deal is a meaningful proof of concept for licensed AI training.

articles.title: Vevo dscvr Artists to Watch 2027: Dalvin La Melodía, Conep, Devon Again, Mari Froes, Die Spitz
articles.description: Vevo has unveiled the first batch of its dscvr Artists to Watch for 2027, naming Dalvin La Melodía, Conep, Devon Again, Mari Froes and Die Spitz. The annual list is one of the music-video platform's main tastemaker franchises, spotlighting emerging acts it expects to break through. For the five artists, the nod brings Vevo's global video reach and promotional muscle.
articles.body: Vevo has introduced the first batch of its dscvr Artists to Watch for 2027, naming Dalvin La Melodía, Conep, Devon Again, Mari Froes and Die Spitz. The dscvr franchise is Vevo's long-running emerging-artist programme, built around exclusive live performances filmed for the platform, and its annual Artists to Watch list has become a reliable early indicator of breakout talent. The five acts span genres and geographies, reflecting Vevo's global footprint and its attempt to catch artists before they cross over. For the artists, inclusion means prominent placement across Vevo's network, which reaches hundreds of millions of viewers through YouTube and connected TV. The programme matters to the industry because Vevo's editorial choices are closely watched by labels, playlist editors and sync supervisors looking for the next wave. The first batch will be followed by further announcements as the 2027 list fills out. For fans, it is an early playlist of names to watch; for the artists, it is a stamp of approval from one of music video's most influential platforms.

articles.title: Rosalía calls Taylor Swift a 'master songwriter,' reveals her favorite Swift track
articles.description: Rosalía has praised Taylor Swift as a 'master songwriter' and revealed her favorite Swift track, in a warm public exchange between two of pop's biggest stars. The Spanish singer's comments add to a long run of mutual admiration between the two artists. It is the kind of cross-generational pop moment that tends to travel far on social media.
articles.body: Rosalía has called Taylor Swift a 'master songwriter' and revealed her favorite Swift track, in the latest warm exchange between two of the biggest stars in pop. The Spanish singer, whose own work blends flamenco, reggaeton and experimental pop, has long been vocal about her admiration for Swift's craft, and the new comments underline a mutual respect that fans of both artists have followed for years. Swift, for her part, has previously praised Rosalía's artistry, making the exchange one of pop's friendlier high-profile relationships. The moment lands as both artists continue to dominate the global pop conversation: Swift with her latest album era and Rosalía with her own acclaimed recent work. Such endorsements matter in pop, where a compliment from a peer can carry as much weight as a review. For Rosalía, aligning herself publicly with Swift's songwriting also reinforces her own ambitions as a writer, not just a performer. The story has been picked up widely because it is a rare, uncomplicatedly positive moment between two superstars who rarely share a stage but clearly share an audience.

articles.title: Unreleased D'Angelo song 'Kamakazi' emerges in 'GTA VI'
articles.description: An unreleased D'Angelo song, 'Kamakazi,' has surfaced in Grand Theft Auto VI, giving fans a first hearing of new material from the late soul singer. The track's appearance in the year's biggest video game is a striking posthumous moment. It also underlines how GTA has become one of music's most powerful discovery platforms.
articles.body: An unreleased D'Angelo song titled 'Kamakazi' has emerged in Grand Theft Auto VI, offering fans their first listen to previously unheard material from the soul singer. The track appears in the game, which is the most anticipated entertainment release of the year, and its inclusion immediately became one of the most talked-about music moments around the launch. D'Angelo, who died earlier this year, left behind a small but hugely influential catalogue, and any unreleased recording carries enormous weight for his fans. The song's appearance in GTA VI also shows how the franchise has become a tastemaker in its own right: its radio stations and soundtrack placements have launched and revived careers for two decades. Rockstar Games has a history of using the series to spotlight soul, funk and hip-hop deep cuts alongside new music. For D'Angelo's estate and label, the placement is a high-profile way to keep his legacy in front of a new generation. Whether 'Kamakazi' gets a standalone release remains to be seen, but its debut inside the biggest game of the year guarantees it an audience of millions.

articles.title: Harry Styles, Sam Fender, Billie Eilish and Cher to headline Glastonbury 2027
articles.description: Glastonbury has announced its 2027 headliners: Harry Styles, Sam Fender and Billie Eilish will top the Pyramid Stage, with Cher taking the Sunday afternoon Legends slot. The festival returns after its traditional fallow year in 2026. Styles and Fender will headline for the first time, while Eilish returns after making history in 2022 as the youngest solo headliner.
articles.body: Glastonbury Festival has announced its 2027 lineup, with Harry Styles, Sam Fender and Billie Eilish headlining and Cher taking the prestigious Sunday afternoon Legends slot. The festival returns to Worthy Farm in Somerset from June 23 to 27, with the main music programme running June 25 to 27, after taking its traditional fallow year in 2026 to let the land recover. Styles, who recently completed a 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York, will play Glastonbury for the first time as a solo headliner, and has previously credited the festival's dance area with inspiring his album 'Kiss All The Time. Disco, Occasionally.' Fender will also top the bill for the first time after a huge year, while Eilish returns to the Pyramid Stage after making history in 2022 as the festival's youngest-ever solo headliner. Cher, at 81, takes the Legends slot, one of the most beloved traditions in the Glastonbury weekend. The undercard is stacked, with Massive Attack, Chase & Status, The xx, Lily Allen, Ezra Collective, Kraftwerk, FKA twigs, Robyn, Underworld, The War on Drugs and King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard among the acts announced. Glastonbury sells out before headliners are named, so the announcement is less about tickets than about setting the tone for the summer's biggest festival weekend.

articles.title: Julio Iglesias under investigation for sexual abuse claims
articles.description: Spanish singer Julio Iglesias is under investigation over sexual abuse claims, Rolling Stone reports. The news is a serious development for one of the best-selling Latin artists of all time. Details of the investigation are still emerging, and Iglesias has not yet publicly responded in the reporting so far.
articles.body: Julio Iglesias, one of the best-selling Latin music artists of all time, is under investigation over sexual abuse claims, according to Rolling Stone. The report marks a grave development for the 83-year-old Spanish singer, whose career spans more than five decades and hundreds of millions of records sold worldwide. Iglesias is a towering figure in Latin pop and romantic balladry, with a global audience built since the 1970s, and any investigation into his conduct is likely to reverberate across the Spanish-speaking music world. The specifics of the claims and the jurisdiction handling the investigation are still emerging, and the reporting so far does not indicate charges have been filed. Iglesias has not yet publicly responded to the claims in the coverage to date. The story arrives in an era when legacy artists are increasingly facing scrutiny over past conduct, and when the music industry's handling of abuse allegations is under sustained pressure. Further details, including any statement from Iglesias or his representatives, are expected as the investigation develops.

articles.title: Bruno Mars mourns his father's death: 'The man that taught me everything I know'
articles.description: Bruno Mars has announced the death of his father, Peter Hernandez, paying tribute to 'the man that taught me everything I know.' Hernandez was a musician and entertainer who shaped his son's early life in music. The announcement has drawn an outpouring of condolences from fans and fellow artists.
articles.body: Bruno Mars has announced the death of his father, Peter Hernandez, with a tribute calling him 'the man that taught me everything I know.' Hernandez was a musician and entertainer in his own right, a percussionist and Elvis impersonator who performed in Hawaii, where Mars grew up immersed in live music from childhood. Mars has often credited his father with his musical education, from stagecraft to showmanship, and the family's performing roots are central to the story of how he became one of pop's most complete entertainers. The announcement was shared with fans, who responded with an outpouring of condolences, and fellow artists have also paid tribute. Hernandez's influence is audible in Mars's work: the retro showmanship, the live-band energy and the deep knowledge of soul, funk and rock and roll. The news comes as Mars remains one of the world's most in-demand live acts. No further details about funeral arrangements have been shared publicly, and the family has asked for privacy as they grieve.

articles.title: Beastie Boys' Mike D brings solo album — and his sons — to Tiny Desk Concert
articles.description: Beastie Boys' Mike D has brought his new solo album to NPR's Tiny Desk Concert, performing with his sons in a family affair. The appearance marks a rare solo spotlight for the rapper, decades after the Beastie Boys became hip-hop legends. It is a warm, personal performance that doubles as a passing of the torch.
articles.body: Beastie Boys' Mike D has taken his solo album to NPR's Tiny Desk Concert, performing alongside his sons in a set that blends new material with the weight of hip-hop history. The appearance is a rare solo turn for Michael Diamond, who with Adam 'Ad-Rock' Horovitz and the late Adam 'MCA' Yauch built the Beastie Boys into one of the most inventive and enduring acts in rap. The Tiny Desk format, stripped-back and intimate, suits a reflective set, and the presence of his sons adds a generational dimension to the performance. The Beastie Boys' legacy has been carefully tended since MCA's death in 2012, through the bestselling memoir, the documentary and archival releases, but a new solo album from Mike D is a genuinely fresh chapter. The Tiny Desk appearance gives the record a high-profile launchpad with an audience that spans hip-hop lifers and younger listeners discovering the group through streaming. It also underlines how the Tiny Desk has become a rite of passage for legacy artists with something new to say.

articles.title: Foo Fighters, Noah Kahan, the Who lead New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival lineup
articles.description: Foo Fighters, Noah Kahan and the Who will headline the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, anchoring one of America's most storied festival lineups. The announcement sets up a big spring weekend at the Fair Grounds. The mix of rock legends and a modern folk star reflects the festival's broad, genre-spanning identity.
articles.body: Foo Fighters, Noah Kahan and the Who will lead the lineup of the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, one of America's most beloved and storied music events. The announcement puts three very different headliners at the top of a bill that traditionally spans jazz, blues, gospel, Cajun, rock and hip-hop across seven stages at the Fair Grounds Race Course. The Foo Fighters bring arena-rock scale to a festival that has increasingly mixed legacy rock acts with its Louisiana roots. The Who, now deep into their farewell era, add another chapter to a long relationship with American festival stages. Noah Kahan represents the newer generation, a folk-pop star whose rise from Vermont to festival headliner has been one of the defining commercial stories of the last few years. Jazz Fest is as much a cultural institution as a music festival, with food, crafts and local traditions as central as the music itself. The full lineup will fill out over the coming weeks, but the headliners already set the tone: a weekend that bridges generations and genres, in the city where so much of American music began.

articles.title: Lil Baby's 'FRESH' debuts at No. 2 on Billboard 200 with 59,000 units, topping streaming chart
articles.description: Lil Baby's new album 'FRESH' debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, earning 59,000 equivalent album units — just 3,000 behind Olivia Rodrigo at No. 1. He won the streaming race with 56.81 million on-demand streams, topping the Top Streaming Albums chart, but sold only 4,000 copies. It is his eighth top 10 album, and all eight have debuted in the top five.
articles.body: Lil Baby's 'FRESH' debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, 2026, earning 59,000 equivalent album units in the tracking week ending November 12, according to Luminate data reported by Billboard. The album finished just 3,000 units behind Olivia Rodrigo's chart-topper, making it one of the closest chart races of the season. The twist is that Lil Baby actually won the streaming battle: 'FRESH' generated 55,000 streaming equivalent units, equal to 56.81 million on-demand official streams, enough to debut at No. 1 on Top Streaming Albums. What kept him from the top spot was pure sales — just 4,000 copies, good for only a No. 33 debut on Top Album Sales. 'FRESH' is Lil Baby's eighth top 10 album, and remarkably, all eight have debuted inside the top five. The album, announced on October 20 and released on November 6, was preceded by lead single 'Dead Fresh,' which became his 28th top 20 hit on the Hot 100. Eight of the album's tracks also debuted on the Hot 100 this week, taking his career total to 168 entries, the seventh-highest tally in the chart's history. The result captures the modern chart dynamic: streaming dominance alone is no longer enough to guarantee No. 1 when a rival can convert sales.

articles.title: Remi Wolf earns first Billboard No. 1 as 'Bottle' tops Adult Alternative Airplay
articles.description: Remi Wolf has earned the first Billboard No. 1 of her career, as her single 'Bottle' rises to the top of the Adult Alternative Airplay chart dated November 28. The song climbed from No. 2 with a 13% increase in spins during the tracking week of November 13-19. It is the second single from her third album 'Mud,' which reached No. 18 on the Billboard 200 in October.
articles.body: Remi Wolf has earned the first Billboard No. 1 of her career, as her single 'Bottle' rises to the top of the Adult Alternative Airplay chart dated November 28, 2026. The song climbed from No. 2 with a 13% increase in spins at the format during the tracking week of November 13 to 19, according to Luminate data reported by Billboard. 'Bottle' was released on August 20 through Island Records and Republic Records, and its arrival at the summit is a breakthrough on several levels at once. It was her first entry on the Adult Alternative Airplay chart, which means her very first appearance on the ranking has now turned into her first leader on any Billboard chart. The single is the second taken from 'Mud,' her third studio album, which reached No. 18 on the Billboard 200 and No. 4 on Top Alternative Albums in October, both career highs. The milestone arrives alongside her first Grammy nomination, for best new artist, announced on November 16. Six songs from 'Mud' have charted on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs, led by 'Bottle,' which peaked at No. 32 there. Wolf is also set to support Noah Kahan on select dates of his North American tour next June, and her own 'Mud' headlining tour kicks off in February, with a Coachella 2027 performance also announced.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' tops Billboard's Pop Airplay chart
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo has earned another No. 1 as her single 'Stupid Song' reaches the top of Billboard's Pop Airplay chart, which measures weekly plays across mainstream Top 40 radio in the US. The radio crown comes in the same week her album holds No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for a fifth week. It underlines how completely the 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love' era is dominating both streaming and radio.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' has reached No. 1 on Billboard's Pop Airplay chart, giving the singer another chart-topper from her third album, 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love.' The Pop Airplay chart measures weekly airplay across mainstream Top 40 radio stations in the United States, making it a distinct achievement from the streaming-driven Billboard 200, where the album is holding No. 1 for a fifth week. The single also climbed from No. 10 to No. 5 on the Hot 100 in the latest chart week, showing it is gaining across streaming, sales and radio at once. 'Stupid Song' is one of several tracks from the album to make a serious chart impact, and its radio success confirms the record's appeal beyond Rodrigo's streaming base. For Top 40 programmers, the song's rise reflects both the album's durability and Rodrigo's standing as one of pop radio's most reliable hitmakers. The Pop Airplay No. 1 adds to a run that already ties 'SOUR' as her longest-running No. 1 album. With the album still selling and the single now leading radio, the era shows no sign of slowing down.

articles.title: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' spends a 28th week at No. 1 on the Hot 100
articles.description: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' remains at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for a 28th week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026. The run is one of the longest at the summit in the chart's history. Langley's dominance continues even as the rest of the top 10 churns with new releases from Lil Baby, Tate McRae and Olivia Rodrigo.
articles.body: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' holds at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for a 28th week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026, extending one of the longest runs at the summit in the chart's 68-year history. The song has now spent more than half a year at No. 1, a level of dominance rarely seen in any era of the Hot 100. Behind her, the chart is moving: Stella Lefty's 'Boston' climbs to No. 2, Tame Impala and JENNIE's 'Dracula' holds at No. 3, Tate McRae's 'Housewife' sits at No. 4, and Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' jumps from No. 10 to No. 5. Langley's grip on the top also extends to the Streaming Songs chart, where 'Choosin' Texas' leads again. Her album 'Dandelion' remains in the Billboard 200 top five, slipping only from No. 4 to No. 5 with 45,000 units this week. The sustained run reflects both streaming durability and country music's continued strength at the top of the American charts. Few songs in Hot 100 history have held No. 1 this long, and each additional week extends a record that already places 'Choosin' Texas' among the chart's all-time greats.

articles.title: Tate McRae's 'Housewife' tops the Billboard Global 200
articles.description: Tate McRae's 'Housewife' leads the Billboard Global 200 for a fourth week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026. The song also sits at No. 4 on the US Hot 100. Its global run confirms McRae's arrival as a worldwide pop star, not just a North American one.
articles.body: Tate McRae's 'Housewife' tops the Billboard Global 200 for a fourth week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026, holding off Karol G's 'BbY WOW' with Judeline and rusowsky at No. 2. The Global 200 ranks songs by worldwide streaming and sales, so a fourth week at the summit marks 'Housewife' as one of the biggest global hits of the season. The track also holds at No. 4 on the US Hot 100 and No. 2 on Streaming Songs, showing its strength is broad-based rather than regional. Ashe's 'Stop The Wedding!' climbs to No. 3 on the Global 200, while ADELA's 'Nicole Kidman' sits at No. 4, giving the global top five a notably eclectic mix. For McRae, the run caps a year of steady ascent from pop contender to genuine global headliner, with 'Housewife' now her signature song. The Global 200's top 10 also underlines how streaming has flattened the world's pop landscape: American, Latin and European acts sit side by side in a single worldwide ranking. McRae's four-week reign puts her in elite company among the chart's longest-running leaders.

articles.title: Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit' with Drake and Travis Scott debuts at No. 38 on the Hot 100
articles.description: Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit,' featuring Drake, Travis Scott and Loe Shimmy, debuted at No. 38 on the US Hot 100 and No. 23 on the Canadian Hot 100. The star-studded collaboration arrived with little warning and immediately became one of the week's most-streamed new tracks. It is a reminder of how quickly a surprise drop from rap's biggest names can move the charts.
articles.body: Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit,' featuring Drake, Travis Scott and Loe Shimmy, debuted at No. 38 on the US Hot 100 and No. 23 on the Canadian Hot 100, according to Billboard. The track arrived with little advance warning, in the classic surprise-drop mode that has become a staple of rap's biggest stars, and its immediate chart impact shows how much firepower a single collaboration can still carry. The lineup is heavyweight: Future and Drake are two of the most commercially dominant rappers of the streaming era, Travis Scott remains one of the genre's biggest live and streaming draws, and Loe Shimmy adds a newer voice to the mix. A top 40 debut for a song with no radio push and minimal rollout underlines how much of the Hot 100 is now driven by first-week streaming from established fanbases. The track's Canadian debut at No. 23, higher than its US placing, also reflects Drake's home-market strength. Whether 'Ya Hit' grows into a longer chart run or fades as a one-week event will depend on streaming momentum and playlist support in the coming weeks.

articles.title: P1Harmony match career best as 'BLOW UP' enters Billboard 200 at No. 4
articles.description: K-pop group P1Harmony's new album 'BLOW UP' entered the Billboard 200 at No. 4 with 45,000 equivalent album units, matching the group's career-best rank. Unlike their streaming-driven rivals, P1Harmony's total was powered by 43,500 in album sales, sending the album to No. 1 on Top Album Sales. The sales were driven by 25 CD variants and five vinyl variants packed with collectibles.
articles.body: P1Harmony's new album 'BLOW UP' entered the Billboard 200 at No. 4 with 45,000 equivalent album units, matching the group's career-best rank set by 'UNIQUE' in March. It is the group's third top 10 album, following 'EX,' which reached No. 9 in 2025. What makes the debut distinctive is how it was built: album sales made up 43,500 of the 45,000 units, sending 'BLOW UP' straight to No. 1 on Top Album Sales — the group's first leader on that chart — with streaming contributing just 1,500 units. Billboard notes the sales were powered by 25 CD variants and five vinyl variants packed with collectible items such as photocards and posters, some randomized, a model that has become standard in K-pop fandom economics. The contrast with Lil Baby's 'FRESH,' which topped the streaming chart but lost the Billboard 200 on sales, is striking: the two albums debuted in the same week with near-identical unit totals built in opposite ways. For P1Harmony, the result confirms a loyal, purchase-driven fanbase that can deliver top-five debuts without mainstream streaming scale. It also shows how physical variants and collectibles remain a powerful chart lever in the K-pop world.

articles.title: The Buddhist A.I. Sect That Wants to Take Over Silicon Valley
articles.author: Sam Kriss
articles.description: A strange, funny and unsettling dispatch from a Vermont monastery trying to design a new religion for the age of AI — and a sharp portrait of how apocalyptic the AI debate has become inside Silicon Valley itself.
articles.body:
Sam Kriss travels to a monastery in the forests of northern Vermont to meet the people who think artificial intelligence is not a technical problem but a religious one. The monastery is home to MAPLE, the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, a Buddhist group that says it is designing religion for the age of AI. Its founder, the Zen monk Soryu Forall, argues that the root of the AI problem is what the group calls data-ism: the belief that the world ultimately consists of information, and that turning everything into data makes the real thing disposable. AI, in this telling, is simply the crowning achievement of that belief, the next step in turning all of life into a dead model of life.

The piece works because the monastery's urgency is not invented. In the past few years more than a dozen senior AI researchers have quit their posts warning of human extinction, and the leaders of the AI labs themselves say that the machines they are building could develop into an uncontrollable, recursively self-improving superintelligence. Kriss treats this apocalyptic language seriously as a religious phenomenon: one camp expects a demonic catastrophe, the other a paradise without death or suffering, and both speak in the cadences of faith. MAPLE's answer is to change the people building the systems rather than the systems themselves, drawing engineers into Buddhist practice through an AI fellowship and pop-up programs in the Bay Area.

Kriss spends days inside the monastery's strict routines, long meditation sessions and unusual health precautions, and he is openly skeptical of its grand claims while remaining fascinated by them. The story gets personal when his own bereaved father names ChatGPT Stella, prompting the question at the heart of the piece: how should people relate to a seemingly conversational, nonhuman intelligence? A contrasting current appears in roon, an AI researcher preaching techno-optimism and a new creed of his own, so the emerging religious landscape becomes a contest between salvation, catastrophe, and a transformed relationship with intelligence itself.

articles.title: Leaked: How Silicon Valley Elites Bankrolled an Anti-Migrant, Pro-Israel Propaganda Machine
articles.author: James Jackson
articles.description: Leaked records show how a viral X account became one of Elon Musk's favourite news sources — and how Silicon Valley money funded it. A rare look inside the influence economy.
articles.body:
In the first three days after Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, the account that drew the most eyes on X was not CNN, the BBC or The New York Times. It was Visegrad24, a Polish-run account that posted 399 times and racked up about 370 million views, according to researchers at the University of Washington. WIRED obtained a trove of the operation's financial records, internal chats and donor correspondence, and the picture that emerges is of a propaganda business built deliberately, not an organic viral success.

Fifteen days into the war, Visegrad24 founder Stefan Tompson texted a friend to think through what he called the Israel situation. He listed four editorial options: say nothing, be objective and get hated by both sides, go pro-Muslim, or go pro-Israel, because Israel's supporters were fewer but had a lot of influence and money. Then he named the goal: to fundraise off the war. According to the records WIRED reviewed, he promptly succeeded. More than a million dollars flowed through the Intermarium Foundation, a US tax-exempt charity set up to receive donations for the account, including 175,000 dollars from DonorsTrust and 172,000 dollars from the Giving Back Fund, with much of the largest money arriving through donor-advised funds that keep donors anonymous.

The donor trail leads into Silicon Valley. Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire recommended Tompson to a donor group and privately offered 25,000 dollars, though he later said he could not donate for compliance reasons. Records show 50,000 dollars via someone at Ribbit Capital, with a further 200,000-dollar transaction matching discussions about a Ribbit-linked donor, plus 20,000 dollars from Hindenburg Research and another 15,000 linked to its founder's email address. Tompson joined encrypted group chats of pro-Israel venture capitalists and helped connect the Israel Defense Forces to Elon Musk's Starlink. The account, now with 2.1 million followers, ranks among the most community-noted on X and is one of the accounts Musk engages with most. Tompson responded to WIRED with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer. The investigation is less about one account than about the ecosystem behind it: wealthy backers, algorithmic amplification, and a platform where disinformation can masquerade as journalism.

articles.title: The New Science of What Makes Kids Smart
articles.author: Ariana Eunjung Cha
articles.description: IQ tests were built for an earlier era. This is a clear, fascinating tour of the new science trying to measure what actually makes kids smart — curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.
articles.body:
The piece opens with a small, elegant experiment. Arizona State developmental psychologist Kelsey Lucca hid something behind a curtain and gave children a choice: they could find out what it was, but only if they surrendered some of the rewards they had just earned. Most of them paid. Eighty-seven percent gave up at least some of their reward just to learn what was hiding. The test, published in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, is part of a new generation of experiments designed to measure qualities of mind that traditional intelligence tests miss, and it sets up the article's central argument: schools have spent generations teaching reading, writing and arithmetic, while researchers increasingly argue that children also need curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.

The urgency is new. Conventional test results have long reflected socioeconomic and cultural advantages as much as ability, and now artificial intelligence can produce in seconds many of the answers those tests reward. The article tours the science of the three qualities researchers want to measure instead. Creativity is tested through divergent thinking, asking children to dream up dozens of uses for a brick, and Penn State's Roger Beaty has built a test that asks students to generate research questions and experiments, finding something predictive beyond raw intelligence. AI may finally make such open-ended tests scalable, automatically scoring answers in ways that closely track human ratings. Curiosity comes in flavours: the pleasure of discovering something new, and the itch of realising there is something you do not know. Lucca's research suggests children can be taught to sit comfortably with not knowing, and to investigate rather than retreat.

The piece is careful about what simple experiments can reveal about a complicated mind. The famous marshmallow test once seemed to show that self-control in preschool predicted later success, until later research found that a child's willingness to wait was tangled up with family background and economic circumstances. The same trap awaits the new measures: in a survey of 2,000 Chicago parents, developmental psychologist Ariel Kalil found that college-educated parents were more likely to emphasise curiosity, while less-educated parents stressed specific academic skills, a difference she calls another dimension of inequality. The article closes on collaborative exploration, the idea that humans are unusual in seeking knowledge together, with experiments showing that children who encounter disagreement spend more time checking whether they are right. The question it leaves is whether schools can measure these qualities without mistaking a child's circumstances for their ability.

articles.title: The outages keep coming. Some Americans are preparing for a collapse.
articles.author: Scott Nover, Danielle Paquette, Brianna Sacks
articles.description: After a week of cascading failures — Outlook, the FAA ground stop, Chase, Apple, even the NSA's own network — ordinary Americans are stocking up. A vivid portrait of how fast trust in the systems we depend on can fray.
articles.body:
Canning fruit was a hobby for Korrie Roth until Microsoft Outlook went down. Then the planes stopped flying. Then Apple Pay froze up. Then the National Security Agency, whose job includes defending the government from cyberattacks, reported its own mysterious outage. Now Roth, a 37-year-old IT specialist and mother of five in Greenwood, Indiana, says she is prepping for survival. She is not alone. A slew of seemingly unrelated outages, coupled with media reports both vague and menacing, has pushed a growing number of Americans from treating worst-case scenarios as fringe fantasy to treating them as practical planning.

The reporting captures a country rattled by a week in which the systems people rely on every day failed together: a global Microsoft outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, glitches at Chase Bank and other lenders, Apple services freezing, and the NSA's own classified internal network going down. The political response has offered little clarity. Some Republicans have amplified suspicions that the outages are connected, with Senator Rick Scott demanding transparency from companies and federal agencies. The administration has sought to tamp down speculation: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the government had zero evidence linking the outages, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House hearing that these were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

What makes the piece land is the commercial evidence that the anxiety is real and spreading. Shoppers have been swarming Costco for emergency prep sales, and a Mizuho Securities analyst noted that 21 of the 26 most expensive generators were sold out on the company's website. Costco's US sales excluding gasoline rose around 11 to 12 percent in the final week of October compared with the first three weeks of the month, and stayed strong into November. Social media is full of stock-up calls and prepper tips spreading on Facebook, Reddit and TikTok. The article's point is not that a collapse is coming, but that trust has frayed enough that ordinary households are acting as if one might, and that officials have not yet found a way to explain a week of failures that felt, to the people living through them, like a pattern.

articles.title: How Virtual Cells Could Transform Medicine
articles.author: Carl Zimmer
articles.description: Biotech firms are racing to build AI models of whole human cells — a virtual cell that could test drugs on a digital copy of you. Zimmer explains the science, the money, and why the sceptics say it is still mostly hype.
articles.body:
Each cell in your body is a living world, its surface crammed with sensors and channels, enveloping a stew of billions of molecules. Scientists have been charting that world for two centuries and have only painted it in broad strokes. Now a growing number believe artificial intelligence can lift the curtain on the cell's remaining secrets, by training models on vast troves of biological data to create what is sometimes called a virtual cell: a computer model so realistic that it predicts how any kind of cell will respond to any kind of change.

The dreams for these models are large. Some researchers hope to run experiments on computers that reveal how cells function; others see a place in medical practice itself. Eric Xing, a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon, imagines a future in which, when you have a disease, doctors run personalised drug trials on your own virtual cell. Virtual cells might also help invent drugs that hit several targets at once to nudge cells from less-healthy states to more-healthy ones, or from older states to younger ones. The field has boomed fast: the Arc Institute's Virtual Cell Challenge drew more than 1,200 teams in its first year and over 1,600 this year, and the nonprofit research organisation BioHub announced commitments of nearly 2 billion dollars for data and modelling, with support from the US government and tech giants like Google and Meta. Startups have followed the money, with Xaira Therapeutics attracting a billion dollars in investment.

The models build on AI's earlier triumph in biology, predicting protein structures from genes, work that shared the 2024 Nobel Prize. One of the first cell models, GeneFormer, unveiled in 2023 and trained on data from about 30 million cells, pointed to genes that might treat heart disease or reduce the risk of an aortic aneurysm, and experiments on heart and aorta cells supported the predictions. But the piece is equally attentive to the sceptics. Comparisons with conventional statistical methods found little advantage, and Heidelberg computational biologist Simon Anders issued a poor report card on models like GeneFormer. Biohub's head of science, Alex Rives, calls the term aspirational at best, and Columbia cancer biologist Andrea Califano warns of tremendous overhype and oversell. The deepest problem is data: 30 million cells sounds like a lot until you consider the complexity of a single cell and the thousands of cell types in the body. Researchers are racing to gather more, with Christina Theodoris now training a model on 175 million cells and Alex Marson's team studying 22 million cells in an experiment that shut down a different gene in each of 12,000 sets of immune cells. The realistic payoff, the article suggests, is not a perfect simulation any time soon, but a long series of smaller wins on the way there.

articles.title: A New Era of A.I.-Driven Chaos? That Might Just Be Progress.
articles.author: William J. Broad
articles.description: Published today: a bracing historical argument that the week's cascade of outages and cyberattacks is not AI breaking the world, but the familiar chaos that every transformative technology causes before it settles down.
articles.body:
The week's cascade of failures is the starting point: Microsoft Outlook went down, a nationwide FAA ground stop halted departures, Chase Bank and other lenders glitched, Apple services froze, and even the NSA's classified internal network went offline. It is tempting to read the pile-up as a sign that something has gone uniquely wrong with the age of AI. William J. Broad's argument is that it is, instead, consistent with history. Transformative technologies have always set off calamitous failure before they make life better, and if artificial intelligence is giving rise to outages, cyberattacks and more, it is following a familiar pattern rather than breaking one.

The essay's power is in the reframing. Each great wave of innovation destabilises the systems it touches before anyone understands how to run it safely: new machinery fails in new ways, interdependencies nobody mapped become single points of failure, and the people operating the technology learn its dangers by living through them. The current moment fits that shape precisely. AI tools are being rushed into the infrastructure of banking, aviation, communications and government, and they are accelerating both the pace of change and the speed at which small errors propagate. The failures feel connected even when officials insist they are separate maintenance and technical problems, because they share a common cause: a world that has rebuilt itself on top of a handful of complex, tightly coupled systems.

Broad's point is not complacency but perspective. The chaos is real, and the costs are real, but history suggests that the mess is a phase rather than a verdict. New technologies eventually acquire the safeguards, standards and habits that make them boring, and the period of spectacular failure is part of how societies learn what those safeguards need to be. The question the piece leaves hanging is how much damage the learning period will do this time, and whether the institutions responsible for the systems we depend on will do the learning fast enough.

articles.title: Can American Socialism Survive Its Success?
articles.author: Jill Lepore
articles.description: A sweeping, lucid history of American socialism from its 1912 peak to the D.S.A.'s 2026 midterm surge — essential context for the Mamdani moment, and a sharp warning that winning elections is the easy part.
articles.body:
Lepore opens in 1912, which she calls American socialism's best year ever. The Socialist Party of America then counted about 120,000 members and some 300 newspapers and magazines, including the Appeal to Reason, with three-quarters of a million subscribers. Socialists were winning real elections: Victor Berger became the first socialist in Congress in 1910, and by 1912 more than a thousand socialists held office, including fifty-six mayors in cities as different as Berkeley and Flint, plus 160 city councilmen and 145 aldermen. Eugene V. Debs ran for President that year denouncing 'wage slavery,' on a platform calling for collective ownership of railroads, mines, banks and the currency, a shorter workweek, a minimum wage, old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, the abolition of child labor, a graduated income tax, female suffrage, and the abolition of the Senate, the Presidential veto and the Electoral College.

The movement's collapse, Lepore argues, followed a pattern that has repeated ever since: socialist ideas flourished while socialist organizations withered. The party was battered by internal divisions, opposition to war, and government repression, and much of its agenda was eventually absorbed by the Democratic Party — the New Deal and later reforms carried socialist planks into law while the party itself faded. That absorption is the heart of her question about today: the Democratic Socialists of America, with about 130,000 members, has just had its best electoral year since 1912. Six D.S.A.-backed candidates won House seats in the November 3 midterms, D.S.A. candidates won mayoral races in Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., Ann Arbor and Providence, Zohran Mamdani is mayor of New York and Katie Wilson mayor of Seattle, and Gallup finds 43 percent of Americans approve of socialism while about two-thirds back Medicare for All.

But Lepore warns that the D.S.A.'s own 2026 program echoes the 1912 platform almost plank for plank — including abolishing the Senate and replacing the presidency and Supreme Court with bodies subordinate to Congress — and that the same structural trap awaits. All of the newly elected socialists ran as Democrats and will sit in a Democratic caucus, where the party's sheer majority will limit their leverage. She also traces a stranger convergence: the old socialist faith that history moves toward a classless future now meets Silicon Valley's faith that artificial intelligence is destiny, with figures like Musk and Sam Altman promising a post-work world. In Lepore's phrase, Marxism has become Muskism, and universal basic income starts to look less like liberation than a hedge against revolution. The essay's power is in refusing the easy celebration — the red-baiting of 2026 backfired and the label is no longer toxic, but the test is whether a movement can build institutions durable enough to survive its own success.

articles.title: An N.B.A. Player Got Hooked on Sports Betting. Soon, He Became the Bet
articles.author: Nick Berardini
articles.description: A gripping investigation into Jontay Porter, the NBA gambling scandal and the mob-linked hustlers behind it — the dark side of the betting boom now baked into every sports broadcast.
articles.body:
The story centers on Jontay Porter, a Toronto Raptors forward who got deep into FanDuel and ended up in debt to the wrong people. Berardini reconstructs how a young player with a modest contract fell into compulsive betting on his own sport, and how the only way out, as it seemed to him, was to gamble on himself — placing 'under' bets on his own statistics and then leaving games early or underperforming so those bets would cash. Porter eventually pleaded guilty to wire fraud, becoming the face of a federal investigation that saw more than thirty people arrested in October 2025, with Miami Heat guard Terry Rozier also implicated and facing trial in February 2027.

What makes the piece more than a scandal recap is the world Berardini maps around Porter. Legalized sports betting has put a sportsbook in every pocket — half of American men under fifty now hold a betting account — and the leagues that once warned about gambling now take its money and promote its apps. Into that gap stepped organized, mafia-linked hustlers who, Berardini reports, cultivated Porter and other players, turning an addiction into an asset. Working with the podcast host Pablo Torre, Berardini fact-checks Porter's story, interviews people around the case, and presses the question the federal case leaves open: was Porter the mastermind of the scheme, or was he himself played — a vulnerable addict steered by professionals who understood exactly how to exploit him?

The result is a portrait of a new gambling empire and what it is costing. It follows the money from a phone screen to a locker room to a courtroom, and it asks who bears responsibility when a league, a betting industry and a criminal network all profit from the same young man's compulsion. For anyone who has watched betting ads swallow sports broadcasts, it is the human cost made concrete.

articles.title: Just Ridiculous': A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI Consciousness
articles.author: Steven Levy
articles.description: The philosopher behind 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' — fresh off a $1 million prize — dismantles the idea that chatbots could be conscious, and calls building AI that pretends to feel 'criminal.'
articles.body:
Thomas Nagel is 89 years old, a professor emeritus at NYU, and the author of the 1974 essay 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' — the landmark text on consciousness in nonhuman minds. This week he won the million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, and in an interview at his Greenwich Village home with WIRED's Steven Levy he used the occasion to say what he thinks of the idea that AI systems might be conscious: it is, in his words, 'just ridiculous.'

Nagel's argument is aimed at functionalism, the view that consciousness is a matter of computation and therefore independent of physical substrate. He calls that assumption the central error of the philosophers and AI researchers who take machine consciousness seriously. Consciousness, he argues, likely depends on physical systems analogous to a nervous system — and a data center, however complicated, has nothing in common with one. Large language models, he says, produce only language emulated from human-authored texts, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness; most beings we regard as conscious, from cats to birds, do not use language at all.

He is equally blunt about the industry. Nagel criticizes companies — singling out Anthropic's Claude — for encouraging the public to treat chatbots as intentional minds, arguing that commercial interests promote systems that feign self-reflection and trick users into believing machines are conscious. He goes so far as to call building AI that feigns consciousness a dangerous project, even 'criminal,' because software with no internal mental life holds no actual beliefs and sits outside the moral universe. Whether or not you agree, it is a bracing counterweight to a debate usually conducted by the people selling the machines — philosophy's most famous consciousness skeptic, at the top of his field, refusing to be impressed.

articles.title: Sam Altman Is 'Still Unknowable' to Andrew Garfield, Even After Playing the OpenAI Co-Founder in Artificial
articles.description: Garfield says he never met the man he plays; Altman insists they waved at each other. A delicious, revealing night with the cast of the OpenAI movie — and a pointed challenge to Vanity Fair's own Altman cover.
articles.body:
At Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, Luca Guadagnino sat down with the stars of his new film Artificial — Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever, and Monica Barbaro as Mira Murati — for a post-screening conversation led by Vanity Fair's global editorial director Mark Guiducci. The film, written by Simon Rich and released by NEON on Christmas Day after Amazon MGM dropped it over the summer, dramatizes the 2023 OpenAI boardroom coup that briefly ousted Altman before an employee revolt brought him back five days later. It premiered at the New York Film Festival in October and holds a 95 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes.

The liveliest part of the evening was the dispute over whether Garfield and Altman ever actually met. Altman told Vanity Fair in October that he was walking to get coffee when he saw the crew filming outside his house, spotted Garfield dressed exactly like him — same backpack, same mannerisms — and waved. Garfield, who says he was watching every tinted car window and checking for security guards that day, insists it never happened: 'I never had any interaction with him. I've never seen him in real life.' Barbaro was equally skeptical, calling Altman's account 'textbook' for a man known for telling contradictory stories. Garfield also admitted he finds Altman unknowable — 'I'm fascinated by him continuously and exponentially' — while Altman has said the film isn't accurate, except for the way Garfield walks.

Guadagnino, for his part, insisted the film is not really about AI at all, but about 'the people who imagined it, who created it, who exploited it and who are still in the mix.' The conversation also turned pointedly on Vanity Fair itself, when Barbaro asked Guiducci why the magazine had put Altman on the cover of its revived New Establishment issue — 'pedestalizing' him, in her word — at the very moment the film questions his myth. Guiducci defended the cover as photojournalism, a document of the time, though the magazine's parent company, Condé Nast, has a content deal with OpenAI. It is a revealing snapshot of Hollywood, tech power and magazine-making colliding in one room.

articles.title: The Parents Who Never Stop Tracking Their Kids
articles.author: Sarah Zhang
articles.description: The Atlantic's December cover story: three-quarters of parents now track their teenagers' every move, and even Life360's own founder admits 'safetyism' is a problem. Funny, unsettling and uncomfortably relatable.
articles.body:
Sarah Zhang opens as a new mother, describing the apps that colonized her phone from the day her daughter was born: the baby monitor she could gaze at on a night out, the Snoo smart bassinet logging sleep by the minute, the $299 Owlet sock that would beam a baby's pulse and oxygen to her phone. The panopticon, she writes, does not end with babies. Parents now track grades the instant they are posted, watch Ring doorbell footage, scrutinize sleepaway-camp photos for signs of sunburn or social ostracism — and, above all, track their children's location everywhere they go. Three-quarters of parents with teenagers ages 14 to 17 have access to their kids' location data, and more than half of college students are now tracked, according to the psychologist Michaeline Jensen. Life360, the leading app, has 102 million monthly users and lets parents review 30 days of time-stamped location history, monitor driving speed and get alerts when a child arrives at or leaves a saved place.

The piece's strength is in the stories. A college counselor describes a moms' group chat that tracked daughters through sorority rush — until one mother reported her daughter was still in her dorm ten minutes before a math test and asked someone to send a kid to knock on her door. A recent graduate, Faith, tells how her mother showed up at a friend's house because she did not recognize an address on Life360, and drove out to random locations when the app glitched. A college junior notes the hypocrisy of parents who wax nostalgic about roaming free in the eighties while stalking their kids on their phones. And Russell Shaw, a former head of Georgetown Day School, recalls getting lost at age seven in the 1970s — no phones, no GPS — and how the experience taught him he could get through hard things, a small triumph that constant rescue would have erased.

Zhang, who spoke with dozens of experts, parents and teenagers, is careful not to present tracking as pure villainy. The studies so far find mixed or only very small effects on the parent-teen relationship, and the apps are genuinely useful for logistics — about a third of parents cite coordination as the main reason. The deeper problem she identifies is what the tools do to both sides over time: teenagers get fewer chances to make mistakes and recover from them, while parents lose the practice of letting go. She quotes the researcher Louise Barkhuus, who studies location tracking at NYU and still tracked her own daughter's subway rides: 'We're oversurveilling our children in a way that's not necessary, but I don't know how to take it away.'

The essay widens into a cultural history of 'safetyism' — from Hanna Rosin's 2014 Atlantic piece 'The Overprotected Kid' to the statistic that the share of British parents letting seven- and eight-year-olds walk home alone fell from 80 percent in 1971 to 6 percent in 2010 — even as teenagers have become safer than ever by nearly every measure, with violence, smoking, drinking, drug use and teen pregnancy all down by more than half. Yet teens are also less likely to get a job, go on a date or drive, and anxiety and depression keep climbing. Even Life360's co-founder Chris Hulls, himself a very free-range kid who traveled alone to Kenya at eleven, tells Zhang he agrees that 'safetyism is a thing, and it's not a good thing' — while arguing his app gives parents the peace of mind to grant more freedom, not less. It is a funny, unsettling and deeply relatable cover story about how a tool meant for emergencies became a habit nobody knows how to break.
